text: Sexual Dysfunction SLOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to Define erectile dysfunction Describe risk factors, pathophysiology, investigations and management lines. 1 Definition: Erectile dysfunction (ED), formerly termed impotence, is defined as the failure to achieve or maintain a rigid penile erection suitable for satisfactory sexual intercourse Physiology of erection: The critical process in penile erection activity is the relaxation of the intracavernosal smooth muscle. This process permits increased blood flow into the corpora cavernosa, which fills with blood and compresses the emissary veins, reducing venous outflow. The paraventricular and medial preoptic nuclei of the hypothalamus control this process. Signals travel through the parasympathetic nervous system to the parasympathetic nerves of the S2-S4 sacral plexus and then to the penis via the cavernosal nerves. Nitric oxide released by the cavernous nerve terminals initiates the erectile process, while nitric oxide from endothelial cells acts to maintain it. Nitric oxide stimulates the production of cyclic guanosine monophosphate (GMP) when it enters the smooth muscle. Cyclic GMP activates protein kinase G, which opens potassium channels and closes calcium channels. Low intracellular calcium causes the intracavernosal smooth muscle tissue to relax, increasing arterial flow with simultaneous veno-occlusive activity. This results in a rigid erection with minimal blood flow into or out of the corpora once the erection is established. The phosphodiesterases (PDE) are a class of enzymes that degrade cyclic nucleotides such as cGMP and cAMP. There are over 50 isoenzymes identified to date, and PDE isoenzymes types 2, 3, 4, and 5 have been specifically located in the human corpora cavernosa. When penile phosphodiesterase degrades cyclic GMP, the corporal smooth muscle contracts again, and the process reverses. Pathology arising from any of the above processes can result in erectile dysfunction. 3 Etiology of ED: The cause of ED is often multifactorial. It may be psychological or organic. Psychological ED may be attributed to depression, or performance anxiety Organic causes: Aging is an essential factor contributing to ED. As patients age, cardiovascular diseases, hypertension, and other co-morbidities play an increasingly significant role in this condition. Diabetes mellitus and metabolic syndrome can disrupt the mechanisms of erections on a molecular level Neurological diseases (such as multiple sclerosis), Hormonal causes (hypogonadism, thyroid), Traumatic (e.g., pelvic fractures, spinal cord injuries), Medications (antidepressants, antihypertensives, antipsychotics, opioids, and recreational drugs) 6 Cardiovascular Disease and Erectile Dysfunction Cardiovascular disease is a very significant risk factor for ED. Almost 50% of men with known coronary artery disease have ED. The cavernosal arteries develop blockages from atherosclerotic plaques, resulting in vasculogenic ED and endothelial cell dysfunction Other vascular risk factors are hypertension and diabetes, lifestyle factors (such as smoking, activity level, alcohol intake, and the use of any recreational drugs Endothelial dysfunction the endothelium is a major regulator for vascular homeostasis, producing several signaling molecules, most notably nitric oxide, which promotes vasodilation Endothelial dysfunction is characterized impaired nitric oxide synthesis/ degradation. Such events lead to vasoconstriction 7 Diabetes mellitus The etiology of ED in diabetic men probably involves both vascular and neurogenic mechanisms. Endocrine disorders Hypogonadism that results in low testosterone levels adversely affects libido and erectile function. Hypothyroidism is a rare cause of ED. Medications ED is an adverse effect of some psychotropic drugs and antihypertensive agents, 5-alpha reductase inhibitors and alpha blockers. Smoking Cigarette smoking has been shown to be an independent risk factor. In studies evaluating more than 6000 men, the risk of developing ED increased by a factor of 1.5. 8 Workup: Examination: peripheral pulses and measure blood pressure. Genital examination: testicular size (hypogonadism), signs of infection (such as redness and discharge in acute balanoposthitis), the presence of penile fibrosis or plaques, and phimosis (the inability to retract the foreskin). Hair distribution, breast size (gynecomastia), detailed neurological examination Laboratory investigations: Hgba1c to screen for diabetes mellitus, Lipid profile. Testosterone level, LH and prolactin (in case of suspected hypogonadism) TSH 9 Further Testing Penile biothesiometry: It involves an office screening test for penile neuropathy utilizing skin vibrational threshold sensitivity. The process entails placing a blunt-tipped vibrating probe on the right and left shaft, as well as the glans. Patients are required to indicate when they first sense the tip vibrating, determining their threshold vibrational sensitivity. This value is compared to age-based normal standards after obtaining 5 separate readings at each site and averaging the results. While it does not directly examine erectile nerves, it is a reasonable, safe, and cost-effective office test for penile neuropathy Further Testing Nocturnal tumescence testing (NPT): It proves valuable in distinguishing psychogenic from organic erectile dysfunction. Testing involves measuring the frequency, tumescence (circumference changes), duration, and maximal rigidity of nocturnal erections. Nocturnal erections require complete functioning of the neurovascular axis and typically occur during REM sleep. An average functioning man has between 3 and 6 erections a night, with a mean duration greater than 30 minutes, maximal rigidity greater than 70% at both base and tip, as well as an increase in circumference of over 3 cm at the base and 2 cm at the tip. Men with purely psychogenic ED will typically demonstrate normal NPT tracings, while those with organic problems will show abnormal nocturnal erectile activity. Further Testing: Penile duplex Doppler ultrasound this measures arterial vascular flow and checks for cavernous veno-occlusive dysfunction (venous leak). The ultrasound is typically done by giving the patient an intracavernosal injection of a vasoactive drug, usually 20 μg of prostaglandin E1. Following the injection, the peak systolic velocities (PSV) are measured. A normal value is > 35 cm/s, while a reading of < 25 cm/s suggests arterial insufficiency. Ultrasound can also demonstrate cavernous veno-occlusive dysfunction, often called "venous leak" by patients; this finding represents the failure of penile corporal rigidity despite adequate arterial inflow. Venous leak becomes evident when rapid detumescence occurs despite normal peak systolic and end-diastolic velocities (EDV > 5 cm/s) Further Testing Those are used for patients in whom a site-specific venous leak is suspected--usually for patients who have suffered pelvic/perineal trauma. These tests usually precede corrective vascular surgery. Dynamic infusion cavernosometry and cavernosography Treatment: Oral phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (PDE-5 inhibitors): such as sildenafil, vardenafil, tadalafil, udenafil, avanafil, are usually the first-line treatment of ED. competitively inhibit PDE5, decreasing the degradation of cyclic GMP via phosphodiesterase inhibition, and lead to elevated levels of cytosolic cGMP, decreased intracellular calcium which increases the relaxation of cavernosal smooth muscle and vasodilation, increased intracavernosal arterial blood flow, and penile erection. It is important to note that PDE-5 inhibitors do not initiate the erectile response. Sexual stimulation is required to release nitric oxide from the vascular endothelium and penile nerve endings to commence the erectile process. PDE-5 inhibitors are highly effective and have an overall success rate of up to 76%. Should be taken on an empty stomach The most common side effects are headache, indigestion, nasal stuffiness, and mild visual changes such as temporary light sensitivity or bluish coloration to vision. They should not be used at all with nitrates due to potentially dangerous, profound hypotension, and should be used with caution with antihypertensives and alpha-blockers. Patients who fail PDE-5 inhibitor therapy should try at least one other PDE-5 medication, as up to 50% of initial treatment failures will respond to a different PDE-5 drug. 14 Testosterone supplementation: more effective as a treatment for low libido than for ED. To be combined with oral PDE-5 inhibitors for patients with both ED and hypogonadism. External vacuum devices: are non-surgical option for patients with ED. The outer cylinder of the device is placed over the penis and pressed to the body to create an airtight seal. The patient then uses a small, hand-operated (or battery-powered) vacuum pump to create negative pressure around the penis, which engorges the corpora with blood. Intraurethral prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) pellets also called medicated urethral system for erection or MUSE used as urethral suppositories. The medication is absorbed through the urethra and makes its way to the corpora cavernosa, where it causes muscle relaxation, resulting in an erection. Intracavernosal Injections : Intracavernosal injections of papaverine (an alpha-blocker and vasodilator), prostaglandin E1, phentolamine, and atropine cause smooth muscle relaxation, vasodilation, and erections when injected into the corpora cavernosa. These include papaverine The single agent can be used or a combination of two or more Failure of intracavernosal injection therapy is a good diagnostic indicator of vasculogenic ED. The most serious side effect is priapism (prolonged erection) 15 Penile prostheses: are a surgically invasive treatment typically offered when all other, less intrusive measures fail or are otherwise unacceptable. These devices are surgically inserted into the corpora cavernosa to restore erectile function artificially. There are 2 main types available: malleable and inflatable. The malleable prosthesis is physically manipulatable into a straight or bent position per the patient’s wishes. The inflatable type becomes erect by activating a small pump in the scrotum, which fills the inflatable penile balloon cylinders from a hidden fluid reservoir surgically implanted in the lower abdomen. Penile revascularization surgery is performed in patients with ED following pelvic/perineal trauma who have sustained an isolated vascular injury. Low-intensity shockwave therapy has shown efficacy, particularly in patients with severe ED not responding to PDE-5 inhibitors. Shockwave therapy increases angiogenic factors that promote neovascularization, restore smooth muscle activity, and attract stem cells. Intracavernosal stem cells and platelet-rich plasma therapy are promising but experimental, requiring more investigation. 16 References: Male Sexual Dysfunction, A Clinical Guide, edited by Suks Minhas and John Mulhall StatPearls ,Bottom of Form Erectile Dysfunction, Stephen W. Leslie; Thushanth Sooriyamoorthy, 2024. Medscape Erectile Dysfunction, 2024, Edward David Kim

text: Introduction to Male Infertility SLOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to Define male infertility, Recognize causes of male infertility Evaluate semenogram Recognize investigations to evaluate male infertility and management lines 1 Figure 1: Hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis (source : https://www2.nau.edu/~gaud/bio301/content/hpg.htm) Definition: Infertility is generally defined as the inability to achieve pregnancy after 12 months of regular, unprotected sexual intercourse, or 6 months for women over 35. This definition also include the inability to carry a pregnancy to term, including miscarriages or stillbirths. Of all sexually active couples, 12%–15% are infertile, of which a male component can be identified 50% of the time either in isolation or in combination with a female factor. Idiopathic infertility remains a common diagnosis, with approximately 25% of patients not having an identifiable cause of infertility 3 Causes of Male Infertility Pre-testicular Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism Sperm production is deleteriously affected by a lack of testosterone (from low luteinizing hormone LH) and a lack of a stimulatory effect of Follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) on the Sertoli/germ cell complex. The most common causes of Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism include elevated prolactin, medications, illicit drugs, and pituitary damage. Idiopathic Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism ( Kallmann Syndrome) Idiopathic Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism (IHH) is a rare disorder caused by defects in gonadotropin-releasing hormone, including its action and/or release, in the setting of an otherwise normal HPG axis . While the age and severity of presentation may vary, most commonly patients present during adolescence with failure to go through puberty. Other presenting symptoms may include anosmia. In the presence of anosmia, IHH is referred to as Kallmann syndrome, which affects 1 in 8000–10,000 males. The etiology is likely genetic, and multiple genes have been identified as playing a role in pathogenesis including KAL1. 4 Testicular Varicocele A varicocele is a dilation of the pampiniform plexus likely caused by the absence or incompetence of the venous valves of the internal spermatic vein. It is the most common surgically correctable cause of male infertility. The disruption of the heat exchange mechanism in the testis, causing hyperthermia, is the most likely mechanism. Cryptorchidism Cryptorchidism is a condition where one or both testicles fail to descend from the abdomen into the scrotum before birth. It's also known as undescended testicles. Cryptorchidism is associated with testicular hyperthermia and possible role of genetic defect in the testis. Testicular Cancer Tumors may directly disrupt spermatogenesis by mass effect, by alterations of the endocrine cascade, or by the effects of the inflammatory reaction to the tumor. Ionizing Radiation Ionizing Radiation has direct cytotoxic effect on spermatogenesis Chemotherapy Chemotherapy typically targets rapidly dividing cells and thus has profound effects on the germinal epithelium, with decline in spermatogenesis 5 Genetic causes: It is estimated that 2%–8% of infertile men have an underlying genetic abnormality. The two potential etiologies are Y chromosome microdeletions and karyotypic abnormalities. The most common karyotypic abnormalities are Klinefelter’s (47,XXY) and chromosomal translocations. Y chromosome microdeletions occur in approximately 10% of men with azoospermia or severe oligospermia. Sertoli cell only syndrome is also associated with azoospermia. Testicular Injury Injury to the testicle can be sustained either directly or indirectly. Direct trauma can result in loss of volume of seminiferous tubules and possible obstruction from scarring is one possible cause of decreased fertility. Indirect damage to the testis may be sustained by exposure to infection or inflammation of the testis as with mumps. Infection of the testis with the mumps virus causes inflammation and swelling, which is limited by the tunica albuginea; this in turn leads to atrophy. Approximately 1.5% of postpubertal males with mumps may become infertile . Lifestyle Testicular hyperthermia, increased DNA fragmentation, and/or genetic alterations may be related to smoking, illicit drug use, or excessive heat exposure, or exposure to pesticides and heavy metals (such as lead, mercury, boron, and cadmium), and other pollutants. Antisperm antibodies Can result in Impairment of sperm motility and/or penetration Post-testicular Absence of the Vas Deferens Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens (CBAVD) is a condition strongly related to cystic fibrosis Ejaculatory dysfunction/Seminal Vesicle Dysfunction Ejaculatory duct obstruction is a common etiology of male infertility, occurring in 1%–5% of men presenting with infertility. Causes include cystic fibrosis spectrum disease, calcifications, tuberculosis and other GU infections. With chronic ejaculatory duct obstruction, the seminal vesicles may lose contractility with impaired seminal vesicle emptying during ejaculation. Nervous injury affecting ejaculation may occur at many levels and have a diverse etiology ranging from spinal cord injury to peripheral neural damage. Coital Sexual dysfunction, interference with semen deposition in vagina, lubricants may impair semen parameters. Workup: History: sexual and medical history, including reproductive history, sexual performance, libido, prior biological children produced family history, occupation, systemic diseases history of significant trauma to the pelvis, testicles or head, intake of alcohol, smoking, recreational drugs, medications, steroid abuse, previous chemo/radiotherapy, pubertal development, testicular descent, surgical history involving the scrotum and inguinal regions, exposure to toxic chemicals such as pesticides, loss of body hair, shaving frequency, anosmia (associated with Kallman syndrome), breast enlargement and galactorrhea sexually transmitted infections (STIs), tuberculosis, mumps, scrotal infections such as epididymitis Physical examination: signs of endocrinopathy, gynecomastia, skin, hair distribution, secondary sexual characteristics. Examination of the penis would include a check for hypospadias, phimosis Testicular size should be measured. In an average adult male, the testicular volume should be at least 15 ml, and the length of the testis should be at least 4 cm. The presence or absence of the vas deferens Any clinical abnormalities of the testicles, such as epididymal lesions, varicoceles, and hydrocele Hormonal profile: The endocrine (hormonal) lab test panel would include serum follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), testosterone, luteinizing hormone (LH), prolactin, estradiol raised FSH level is indicative of spermatogenesis abnormalities. 9 Semen analysis: The WHO recommends providing a semen specimen after 2–7 days abstinence Preferably, the specimen should be obtained in a sterile cup via masturbation either at home or in the laboratory. The semen specimen should be evaluated within an hour of collection and stored at room or body temperature until then. Computer-assisted semen analysis (CASA) is an automated method of determining sperm parameters which offers several advantages over manual semen analyses. The most recent WHO guidelines for semen analysis are outlined in the 6th edition of the WHO Laboratory Manual for the Examination and Processing of Human Semen (2021): Semen Volume: >= 1.4 mL (1.3-1.5 mL) Total Sperm Number: >=39 million per ejaculate (35-40 million) Total Sperm Motility: >=42% (40-43%) Progressive Sperm Motility: >=30% (29-31%) Normal Morphology: >=4% (3.9-4%) Sperm Vitality: >=54% (50-56%) 10 The Nomenclature Related to the Pathological Semen Quality as Adapted from the World Health Organization Laboratory Manual for the Examination and Processing of Human Semen, WHO : Aspermia: No ejaculate at all. Asthenozoospermia: <30% progressively motile spermatozoa. Absolute asthenozoospermia is when no sperm moves at all, but they are still viable and not dead. Azoospermia: No spermatozoa in the ejaculate. Cryptozoospermia: Spermatozoa absent from fresh preparation but observed in a centrifuged pellet. Leukospermia: >1 million white blood cells/mL ejaculate (also called pyospermia and leukocytospermia). Necrospermia or Necrozoospermia: Complete when all the sperm are dead on a fresh semen sample; incomplete if 5%-45% are still viable. Normospermia: All semen parameters within the acceptable reference limits. Oligozoospermia: Sperm concentration <15 million/mL; total sperm number <39 million/ejaculate. Severe if <5 million/mL. Oligo-astheno-teratozoospermia: Disturbance of all 3 parameters. Teratozoospermia: <4% morphologically normal spermatozoa. 11 Other tests: DNA integrity test: assesses the degree of sperm DNA fragmentation. The test should be done in those with recurrent miscarriages.[94] Genetic Screening: chromosomal testing may be indicated with azoospermia or severe oligozoospermia, Imaging: Ultrasound is the initial radiological method that is used to evaluate the testis. of Scrotal ultrasound is required to identify testicular size, pathologies such as spermatoceles, varicoceles, absence of the vas, or the presence of any testicular masses Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has allowed this noninvasive diagnostic tool to further evaluate testicular function. Testis biopsy with cryopreservation of sperm is a procedure performed in men with azoospermia 12 Treatment: Lifestyle Changes These changes include stopping smoking, limiting or eliminating alcohol intake, adopting a more nutritious diet, weight loss measures if obese, eliminating illegal and recreational drug use, minimizing prescription drugs, avoiding exposure to pesticides and heavy metals Antioxidants They have limited beneficial effects on sperm quality or male infertility. Antioxidants reduce the effects of oxidative stress on semen and sperm and include L-carnitine, coenzyme Q10 , zinc, vitamins C and E , selenium, and Folic acid Hormonal therapies Aromatase inhibitors have shown an ability to improve semen parameters and hormonal parameters They are most useful when testosterone levels are normal but estrogens are relatively high. Both the steroid-based (testolactone) and nonsteroidal (anastrozole and letrozole) drugs appear to have equivalent efficacy. Clomiphene It is an antiestrogen and, in small doses (25 mg every other day up to 50 mg daily), can increase gonadotropins (FSH and LH) and stimulate spermatogenesis, making it potentially useful in idiopathic cases of male infertility. It works by inhibiting the estradiol negative feedback response to the hypothalamus, which results in a higher release of LH, causing higher testosterone levels. Tamoxifen It is a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) that competes with the hormone for binding sites, acting as a competitive inhibitor. By selectively blocking hypothalamic estrogen receptors, tamoxifen stimulates GnRH secretion, greatly increasing FSH and LH levels and ultimately promoting spermatogenesis. Gonadotropic Therapy The use of gonadotropin therapy in most men with idiopathic infertility is controversial. Results are better when gonadotropins are used to correct specific pituitary and hypothalamic disorders. Successful gonadotropin therapy typically consists of some combination of human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG), LH, FSH, GnRH, and human menopausal gonadotropin (HMG). HCG acts similarly to LH but is cheaper and has a longer half-life. HMG contains both FSH and LH and works similarly to GnRH. FSH stimulates Sertoli cell activity and sperm production. Surgical treatment For varicocele and vasal injury/obstruction Assisted reproductive treatment (ART): Many types are available as in vitro fertilization (IVF) and intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI). ICSI involves the use of a microscope to inject a single sperm taken from the male partner directly into an egg from the female partner that has been surgically extracted. The fertilized eggs are implanted into the uterus of the female partner. References: Sijo J. Parekattil Sandro C. Esteves Ashok Agarwal, Male Infertility Contemporary Clinical Approaches, Andrology, ART and Antioxidants Second Edition StatPearls,Bottom of Form Male Infertility, Stephen W. Leslie; Taylor L. Soon-Sutton; Moien AB Khan, Last Update: February 25, 2024 WHO guidelines for semen analysis are outlined in the 6th edition of the WHO Laboratory Manual for the Examination and Processing of Human Semen (2021)

text: Basic skin lesions & skin examination & dermatologic therapies 1 SLOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1 Describe the anatomy of the skin, and epidermal appendages 2 Describe the ultrastructure of the dermo-epidermal junction 3 Describe abnormalities of cutaneous histopathology 4 Describe the main functions of the skin 5 Define the vehicles of topical preparations 6 Describe cutaneous signs (initial and secondary lesions) and give examples 2 Functions of the skin: 1-Maintaining a Barrier The most obvious function of the skin is to maintain a barrier that prevents the loss of fluids, electrolytes, and other molecules from within the body, while also preventing penetration by microorganisms, toxic materials, and UV radiation. The stratum corneum is the key structure for barrier function. Protection against UV radiation occurs through several phenomena, including photon scattering in the stratum corneum and photon absorption by underlying melanin. 2- Thermoregulation Temperature regulation occurs primarily through evaporative cooling following eccrine sweating and through vasodilation and vasoconstriction. The skin and subcutaneous fat also act as insulator. Arteriovenous anastomoses, provide direct connections between arterial and venous plexuses. These anastomoses are prominent in areas exposed to maximal cooling, such as the volar surfaces of the hands and feet, lips, nose, and ears. 3-Interpersonal Communication: Beauty, Attention, and Self-Identity The skin plays an important role in interpersonal communication by conveying beauty to others, attracting attention, and contributing to the development and expression of self-identity. 4- Sensation: The skin contains nerve endings that detect sensations like touch, temperature, pain, and pressure. These sensory receptors help us perceive and react to the external environment. 5- Excretion: The skin excretes waste products, such as sweat, which contains water, salts, and small amounts of other waste products. 6- Absorption: The skin can absorb certain substances, including some medications and chemicals. 7- Vitamin D synthesis: When exposed to sunlight, the skin synthesizes vitamin D, which is essential for calcium absorption and bone health. 3 Structure of the skin: Skin is composed of three layers: the epidermis, dermis, and subcutaneous fat (panniculus). The outermost layer, the epidermis, is composed of viable keratinocytes covered by a layer of keratin, the stratum corneum. The principal component of the dermis is the fibrillar structural protein collagen. The dermis lies on the panniculus, which is composed of lobules of lipocytes separated by collagenous septa that contain the neurovascular bundles. There is considerable regional variation in the relative thickness of these layers. The epidermis is thickest on the palms and soles, measuring approximately 1.5 mm. It is very thin on the eyelid, where it measures less than 0.1 mm. The dermis is thickest on the back, where it is 30–40 times as thick as the overlying epidermis. The amount of subcutaneous fat is generous on the abdomen and buttocks compared with the nose and sternum, where it is extremely thin. Eccrine and apocrine glands, ducts, and pilosebaceous units constitute the skin adnexa. Figure 1: Anatomy of the skin (Andrews' Diseases of the Skin 14th Edition) Epidermis In humans, the epidermis contains four major resident populations: keratinocytes, melanocytes, Langerhans cells, and Merkel cells. The epidermis can be divided into the innermost basal layer (stratum germinativum), the malpighian or prickle layer (stratum spinosum), the granular layer (stratum granulosum), and the horny layer (stratum corneum). On the palms and soles, a pale clear to pink layer, the stratum lucidum, is noted just above the granular layer. Keratinocytes, the major population, are epithelial cells that originate from a stem cell pool situated in the basal layer; cells that leave this pool then differentiate as they migrate upward, ultimately forming the laminated stratum corneum. Under normal conditions, differentiated keratinocytes require about two weeks to exit the nucleated compartment and another two weeks to move through the stratum corneum. Melanocytes, manufacture the light-absorbing pigment melanin, which plays a major role in protecting the skin from the harmful effects of ultraviolet (UV) radiation . Langerhans cells play a critical role in antigen presentation during the regulation of immunity . Dermis Beneath the epidermis, the vascularized dermis provides structural and nutritional support. The dermis is composed of a glycosaminoglycan gel held together by a fibrous connective tissue matrix containing collagen and elastin. Vascular structures, accompanied by nerves and mast cells, course through the dermis to provide nutrition, recirculating cells, and cutaneous sensation. The dermo-epidermal junction The junction of the epidermis and dermis is formed by the basement membrane zone (BMZ). Ultrastructurally, this zone is composed of four components: the plasma membranes of the basal cells with the specialized attachment plates (hemidesmosomes); an electron-lucent zone called the lamina lucida; the lamina densa (basal lamina); and fibrous components including anchoring fibrils, dermal microfibrils, and collagen fibers in the sub-lamina densa. Type IV collagen is the major component of the basal lamina. Type VII collagen is the major component of anchoring fibrils. The two major hemidesmosomal proteins are BP230 (bullous pemphigoid antigen 1) and BP180 (bullous pemphigoid antigen 2, type XVII collagen). Laminin 332 (formerly called laminin 5) is a component of the lamina lucida/lamina densa interface. Figure 2: Structure of the epidermis (Dermatology, 5th Edition By Jean L. Bolognia, 2024) Skin appendages (Adnexa) Hairs: The hair structure divides into the hair shaft and hair follicle. The hair shaft is the portion of the hair that is visible on the outside of the skin. It is made up of cuticle cells that surround the cortex, with a central medulla present in thicker hair. The hair follicle is the primary structure for hair growth and divided into three segments: Infundibulum, Isthmus, and inferior segment. The infundibulum comprises the portion from the epidermal invagination to the level of the ductal opening of the sebaceous gland. The isthmus is the portion from the opening of the sebaceous gland to the insertion of the arrector pili muscle. The inferior segment is the growing portion of the follicle. 7 Nails: The nail unit includes the nail plate, nail folds, and nail matrix., and nail bed. The nail matrix is the germinative zone where stem cells divide, and produce keratin for the formation of the nail. The nail plate is the visible portion of the nail that is rigid and composed of compact keratinocytes. The nail plate is curved and fits tightly into the proximal and lateral nail folds. The nail bed is the portion of the skin beneath the nail plate. Sebaceous Glands Sebaceous glands are part of the pilosebaceous unit, and there are typically multiple sebaceous glands per hair follicle. Sebaceous glands are made up of lobules and ducts. They are true exocrine holocrine glands found in all areas of the skin except for the palms, soles, and lips. The lobules are made up of sebocytes that produce sebum. These glands are pear-shaped, and their duct, the pilosebaceous canal, opens into the upper third of the hair follicle. Sweat Glands The sweat glands categorize as either eccrine and apocrine glands. Eccrine is the most common of the sweat glands, distributed all over the body except the lips and part of the external genitalia. Apocrine glands are limited to the axilla, areola, nipple, skin around the anus, and external genitalia and have an odor. Histologically, the eccrine sweat glands are present in the dermis and upper portion of the hypodermis. There is a secretory portion and a duct portion. The secretory portion appears coiled, and is surrounded by myoepithelial cells that contract to help with the secretory process. Histologically, the apocrine glands are not as coiled and found in the dermis and subcutaneous fat. Like the eccrine glands, the apocrine glands have a secretory and excretory duct portion. These glands are hormonally controlled and become active at puberty. The excretory duct opens into the hair follicle. 8 Cutaneous Signs Typically, most skin diseases present with lesions that have distinct characteristics. The original lesions are known as the primary lesions. They may continue to full development or be modified by regression, trauma, or other extraneous factors, producing secondary lesions. Primary Lesions Primary lesions are of the following forms: macules (or patches), papules (or plaques), nodules, tumors, wheals, vesicles, and bullae. 9 Macules Macules are variously sized (but less than 1 cm), circumscribed changes in skin color, without elevation or depression (nonpalpable). They may be circular, oval, or irregular and may be distinct in outline or may fade into the surrounding skin. Patches A patch is a large macule, 1 cm or greater in diameter, as may be seen in nevus flammeus or vitiligo. Papules Papules are circumscribed, solid elevations with no visible fluid, varying in size from a pinhead to 1 cm. They may be flat topped, dome-shaped, verrucous or umbilicated. Papules are generally centered in the dermis. They may be of soft or firm consistency. The surface may be smooth or rough. If capped by scales, the eruption is called papulosquamous. Plaques A plaque is a broad papule (or confluence of papules), 1 cm or more in diameter. Nodules Nodules are morphologically like papules but are larger than 1 cm in diameter. Nodules most frequently are centered in the dermis or subcutaneous fat. Vesicles (Blisters) Vesicles are circumscribed, fluid-containing elevations 1–10 mm in size . They may be clear from serous exudate or red from serum mixed with blood. Bullae They differ from vesicles only in size, being larger than 1 cm . Bullae may be located superficially in the epidermis, so their walls are flaccid and thin and subject to rupture spontaneously or from slight injury.When subepidermal, the bullae are tense, do not rupture easily, and are often present when the patient is examined. 10 Secondary Lesions Secondary lesions are of many types; the most important are scales, crusts, erosions, ulcers, fissures, and scars. Pustules Pustules are small elevations of the skin containing purulent material, and are like vesicles in shape. Scales Scales are dry or greasy laminated masses of keratin. The body ordinarily is constantly shedding imperceptible tiny, thin fragments of stratum corneum. When the formation of epidermal cells is rapid or the process of normal keratinization is disturbed, pathologic exfoliation results, producing scales. These scales vary in size; some are fine, delicate, and branny, as in tinea versicolor, whereas others are yellow and greasy in seborrheic dermatitis, fish-like as in ichthyosis, collarette as in pityriasis rosea, and others are stratified/ lamellar as in psoriasis. Crusts (Scabs) Crusts are dried serum, pus, or blood. Fissures A fissure is a linear cleft through the epidermis or into the dermis. Erosions Loss of all or portions of the epidermis alone, produces an erosion. It may or may not become crusted, but it heals without a scar. Ulcers Ulcers are rounded or irregularly shaped excavations that result from complete loss of the epidermis plus some portion of the dermis. Ulcers heal with scarring. Scars Scars are composed of new connective tissue that has replaced lost substance in the dermis or deeper parts resulting from injury or disease, as part of the normal reparative process. Scars may be thin and atrophic, or the fibrous elements may develop into hypertrophic scars or keloids. 11 Atrophy: It is thinning of skin due to thinning of epidermis or dermis or both. Atrophic skin is thin, wrinkled, transparent and fragile. Lichenification: It is a descriptive term of 3 criteria: Thickening of skin, Hyperpigmentation and Accentuated skin markings. Skin lichenification is a feature of chronic eczema Specific Initial Lesions: Wheals (Hives) Wheals are evanescent, edematous, plateau-like elevations of various sizes. They are usually oval or of arcuate contours, pink to red, and surrounded by a “flare” of macular erythema. The wheal is the prototypic lesion of urticaria. Scutulum: It is specific for favus. It is cup shaped structure with concavo-convex surfaces, golden yellow in colour and stuck to scalp. Comedones: It is specific to acne. Comedones are essentially a buildup of keratinocytes and sebum within a hair follicle. Tunnel (Burrow): It is specific for scabies. It is a curved line due to burrowing of female mite to skin. Herald patch: It is specific for Pityriasis rosea. It is a patch that has 3 concentric zones: Central café au lait zone, Intermediate collarette scales, Peripheral erythematous zone. 12 Skin signs (Dermatology, 5th Edition By Jean L. Bolognia, 2024) General Diagnosis History Knowledge of the patient’s age, health, occupation, ethnic background, hobbies, diet, recent travel, living conditions, and a complete drug history is important. The family history of similar disorders and other related diseases may be useful. For the presenting dermatosis one should acquire about the onset, duration, and course of the disease and the response to previous treatment. A complete medical history that includes other medical diagnoses of the patient is essential. Certain skin diseases are specific to or associated with other conditions. Habitation in certain parts of the world predisposes to distinctive diseases for that geographic locale, as in case of leprosy. Sexual practices may be relevant, as in genital ulcer diseases and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection. 19 Examination Examination should be conducted in a well-lit room. Natural sunlight is the ideal illumination. The entire eruption must be seen to evaluate distribution and configuration. This is optimally done by having the patient completely undress and viewing from a distance to take in the whole eruption at once. After the patient is viewed at a distance, individual lesions are examined. 20 Major Distribution Patterns Disseminated vs localized vs solitary Unilateral vs bilateral Symmetric vs asymmetric Sun-exposed sites vs sun-protected sites Flexural vs extensor surfaces Intertriginous/large body folds Acral (hands, feet, ears, nose) Palmoplantar Seborrheic region (head and neck, upper trunk) Periorificial Mucosal (mouth, anogenital) “Linear” Dermatomal or zosteriform 21 Lesions in a line are called linear, and they may be confluent or discrete. Lesions may form a complete circle with normal-appearing skin centrally (annular) or a portion of a circle (arcuate), or may be composed of several intersecting portions of circles (polycyclic). Round lesions may be small, like drops, called guttate; or larger, like a coin, called nummular. The Koebner phenomenon or Köbner phenomenon, also called the isomorphic response, is the appearance new skin lesions of a pre-existing dermatosis on areas of cutaneous injury in otherwise healthy skin during disease activity. It occurs in Psoriasis, Vitiligo, and Lichen planus. A pseudo-Koebner response occurs with infections arising in an area of trauma, as with Molluscum contagiosum, and verruca plana. Hair, Nails, and Oral Mucosa Hair Affection Hair affection may be in the form of involvement of hair-bearing areas by certain skin disorders, diffuse hair loss, or loss of hair within a skin lesion. Nail Changes Some skin disorders cause characteristic changes of the nails, as pitting seen in psoriasis and alopecia areata. In addition, the nails and adjacent structures may be the sole site of pathology, as in candidal paronychia. Oral Mucosa Examination The complete skin examination includes examination of the oral mucosa. Oral lesions are characteristically found in viral syndromes (exanthems), lichen planus, HIV, and autoimmune bullous diseases (pemphigus vulgaris). 23 Investigations Wood’s Lamp A Wood’s lamp emits primarily ultraviolet A radiation with a peak wavelength of 365nm. It is used to assist in the diagnosis of pigmentary disorders and infectious diseases . A Wood’s lamp examination is performed in a dark room, with the lamp held 4–5 inches from the area that is to be illuminated. Findings in different skin conditions are as follows: • Vitiligo: Chalk-white • Corynebacterium minutissimum (erythrasma): Coral red • Pityriasis (tinea) versicolor : golden -Yellowish • Tinea capitis due to Microsporum spp. : green • Favus due to Trichophyton schoenleinii : Blue–white 24 Dermoscopy This is a non-invasive skin examination technique that uses a dermatoscope, a handheld device, to visualize subsurface skin structures not readily seen with the naked eye. A dermatoscope is a specialized instrument with a magnifying lens and light source (polarized or non-polarized) that illuminates the skin and reduces surface reflection, allowing for better visualization of deeper skin layers. Skin Biopsy The histopathological findings include: Acantholysis Separation of cell - cell connections (desmosomes) between keratinocytes leading to single, rounded keratinocytes. Seen in pemphigus variants. Acanthosis Thickening of epidermis, with elongated rete ridges usually extend into dermis. Can be regular as in psoriasis (all rete pegs at roughly the same level) or irregular as in lichen planus (rete pegs at different levels of the papillary dermis) Hypergranulosis Thickening of the stratum granulosum. Hyperkeratosis Thickened cornified layer (stratum corneum) Either orthokeratotic (typically compact keratin with no nuclei) or parakeratotic (nuclei in cornified layer) Parakeratosis Retention of nuclei in the stratum corneum. Usually associated with thinning or loss of granular layer (Hypo-or a -granulosis) Spongiosis Intraepidermal edema causing splaying apart of keratinocytes in stratum spinosum. 26 Potassium Hydroxide (KOH) Preparation of Scales Microscopic examination of scale (stratum corneum), obtained via scraping with a metal blade or glass slide and mounted in potassium hydroxide (KOH), is commonly performed to confirm superficial cutaneous fungal infections For onychomycosis, both nail plates and subungual debris are examined. Treatment Topical medications are fundamental in the armamentarium of dermatologic therapeutics, offering the ability to deliver treatment directly to the skin while limiting systemic side effects. Quantity of Application In general, topical medications should be applied to the skin as a thin layer. A thicker layer of medication does not result in enhanced penetration or additional therapeutic benefit. One gram of cream covers a ~10cm × 10cm area of skin. A practical guide to quantifying the amount of ointment necessary to treat different areas of the body is the “fingertip unit” (FTU). One FTU is equal to ~0.5g. The appropriate amount to treat the entire body of an adult man is ~20g. About ~0.5FTU (0.25g) can treat an area equivalent to one side of an extended (“flat”) hand. Types of topical preparations: Solution: Water or alcoholic lotion containing a dissolved powder. Lotion: Usually considered thicker than a solution and more likely to contain oil as well as water or alcohol. A shake lotion separates into parts with time so needs to be shaken into suspension before use. Cream: Thicker than a lotion, a 50/50 emulsion of oil and water. Ointment: Semi-solid, 80% oil, Greasy, protective, and occlusive. Gel: Aqueous or alcoholic monophasic semisolid emulsion, often based on cellulose and liquefies upon contact with skin. Paste: A concentrated suspension of oil, water and powder. Aerosol foam or spray: A solution with pressurized propellant. Powder: Solid, for example, talc (a mineral) or corn starch (vegetable). Solid: Antiperspirant or sunscreen stick. May melt on reaching body temperature (eg, a suppository). Effects of topical preparations: Antipruritic Agents: Topical antipruritic agents may help reduce the urge to scratch/itch, as topical corticosteroids Keratolytic agents reduce the thickness of the stratum corneum via elimination of squames. This can be beneficial in diseases characterized by reduced desquamation or accelerated epidermal proliferation. Examples include salicylic acid and urea. Moisturizing agents (emollients): Moisturizers restore and help maintain water and oils in the skin. Moisturizers typically contain glycerin, mineral oil, or petrolatum and are available as lotions, creams, and ointments. Astringents are liquid drying agents that shrink and contract the skin. The most commonly used astringent solution is aluminum acetate solution. Anti-inflammatory agents: Corticosteroids are the main topical medications used to relieve inflammation of the skin. Tar preparations are noncorticosteroid anti-inflammatory agents, which are byproducts of coal manufacturing. They slow skin cell division and are useful in treating disorders that cause excessive skin production (scaling) such as psoriasis. Anti-infective agents: include topical antibacterial preparations, Topical antifungals, topical antivirals and antiparasitic. Iodine is used to prepare the skin for surgery. Gentian violet is used when an inexpensive antiseptic is needed. Silver preparations (such as silver sulfadiazine) are often used in treating burns and ulcers and have strong antimicrobial properties. Topical compresses: Topical compresses, particularly are used to soften and loosen crusts on the skin, making them easier to remove. They also promote drainage, reduce inflammation, and can help deliver medication to the affected area. Diluted Potassium permanganate acts as a strong oxidizing agent with disinfectant and astringent properties. How does the nature of the dermatosis influence choice of topical formulation? • For wet or oozy skin conditions — creams, lotions, and drying pastes • For dry, scaly skin conditions — ointments References Andrews' Diseases of the Skin, Clinical Dermatology, 14th Edition, Elsevier Dermatology, 5th Edition By Jean L. text: Alopecia Hair cycle The timing of the phases of the hair cycle and its overall duration varies between species, between follicles in different regions of the skin in the same species . Anagen: period of active hair growth, the duration of this phase is responsible for determining the final length of the hair. Under normal circumstances, 80–90% of hair follicles on the human scalp are in anagen at any one time. It may range from few weeks and may continue for several years. Hair cycle Catagen: At the end of anagen, epithelial cell division declines and ceases, and the follicle enters an involutionary phase known as catagen. During catagen, the proximal end of the hair shaft keratinizes to form a club‐shaped structure and the lower part of the follicle involutes by apoptosis . Telogen: The period between the completion of follicular regression and the onset of the next anagen phase is termed telogen. The club hair lies within an epithelial sac to which it is attached by tricholemmal keratin. Hair cycle Exogen: The club hair lies within an epithelial sac to which it is attached by tricholemmal keratin. The club hair is eventually shed through an active process termed exogen. Kenogen: In the human scalp, hair follicles may remain in a state of latency, also known as kenogen, for a pro longed period after the club hair is shed . Rate of hair growth: Published rates of scalp hair growth in humans vary between 0.3 and 0.5 mm per day, slightly faster in adult women than men but greater in prepubertal boys than girls. Androgen‐stimulated hair growth : The growth of obvious facial, trunk and extremity hair in the male, and of pubic and axillary hair in both sexes, is dependent on androgens. The development of such hair at puberty is, in parallel with the rise in levels of androgen from testicular, adrenocortical and ovarian sources, which occurs in both sexes and is somewhat steeper in males. Alopecia areata Alopecia areata is a common, chronic, inflammatory disease that causes non‐scarring hair loss. The incidence rate was 0.1–0.2% with a projected lifetime risk of 1.7%. Alopecia areata occurs in all ethnic groups. The onset of alopecia areata may occur at any age. However, in most affected individuals the first episode occurs before the age of 40, with the peak age of onset between the second and fourth decades. The frequency of alopecia areata is probably the same in both sexes and in all races. Alopecia areata is an autoimmune disease : There is an increased frequency of other autoimmune diseases in patients with alopecia areata. There is an increased frequency of organ‐specific autoantibodies in patients with alopecia areata. Serum antibodies to hair follicle tissue also occur with increased frequency in alopecia areata The pathology is characterized by infiltration of hair bulbs by activated T‐lymphocytes. In animal models of alopecia areata, the depletion of CD4 and CD8 T cells results in hair regrowth • Alopecia areata shares genetic associations with several autoimmune diseases, particularly with genes of the major histocompatibility complex (MHC). Pathogensis There is a very low or absent expression of MHC class I proteins (HLA‐A, ‐B, ‐C) in the lower part of the follicular epithelium. Hair follicle is an immunologically privileged site. In individuals genetically predisposed to develop alopecia areata, pro inflammatory signals such as interferon‐γ (IFN‐γ) upregulate the expression of MHC proteins and NK‐cell‐activating ligands, leads to the collapse of immune privilege and attack by CD8+ cells. High frequency of a positive family history in affected individuals with AA . In most reports, this ranges from 10% to 20% of cases. Clinical features The characteristic initial lesion of alopecia areata is a circum scribed, hairless, smooth patch . The skin within the bald patch appears normal or slightly reddened. Short, easily extractable broken hairs, known as exclamation mark hairs, are often seen at the margins of the bald patches during active phases of the disease . The scalp is the first affected site in most cases, but any hair bearing skin can be affected. An intriguing feature of alopecia areata is the sparing of white hairs. In patients with grey hair, which is an admixture of pigmented and non‐pigmented hair, the disease process appears preferentially to affect pigmented hair, so that non‐pigmented or white hair is spared. (is probably the explanation for historical accounts of people ‘going white overnight’). Sparing of white hair is a relative phenomenon and it is clear that the white hairs, although less susceptible to the disease, are not immune. Dur ing the regrowth phase hairs may be non‐ or hypopigmented . Nail in alopecia areata In 10–15% of cases of alopecia areata the disease also involves the nails, usually in the context of severe hair loss. Classically, alopecia areata causes fine stippled pitting of the nails ,but some cases show less well‐defined roughening of the nail plate (trachyonychia) or a non‐specific atrophic dystrophy. Associated with poor prognosis. Clinical types Patchy alopecia Reticular type Alopecia totalis , subtotalis. Alopecia universalis. Ophiasis (alopecia areata of the occipital, temporal and parietal areas) Sisaipho.( alopecia areata sparing occipital, temporal and parietal areas ) The diffuse form of alopecia areata . A scoring system, the severity alopecia tool (SALT) has been devised to assess the severity. Poor prognostic signs Alopecia totalis. Alopecia universalis. Ophiasis Long standing disease. Early onset. Positive family history. Associated nail disease. Associated auto immune diseases. Associated diseases Several autoimmune diseases including thyroiditis, Lupus erythematosus. Vitiligo Psoriasis. Type 1 diabetes . Atopic dermatitis. Differential diagnosis Causes of non cicatrical alopecia: Non inflammatory tinea capitis. Trichotillomania. Diffuse hair loss due to systemic lupus. Patchy hair loss with secondary stage syphilis. Diffuse hair loss due to systemic disease. Treatment In limited patchy alopecia, a potent topical steroid (e.G. Clobetasol) treatment should be continued for at least 3 months. Intralesional steroids injection is an effective treatment in patchy alopecia areata. A depot steroid (hydrocortisone acetate 25 mg/ml or triamcinolone acetonide 5–10 mg/ml). Topical minoxidil and anthralin (dithranol), have been advocated in patients with limited patchy alopecia. Oral corticosteroids. Treatment Contact immunotherapy: the patient is sensitized to a potent allergen by its application to a small area on the scalp and the same allergen is then applied to the scalp, usually at weekly intervals, in a concentration sufficient to induce a mild contact dermatitis ex: dinitrochlorobenzene (DNCB), squaric acid dibutyl ester (SADBE) and diphenylcyclopropenone (DPCP). PUVA (oral or topical psoralen). Systemic JAK inhibitors: ex: baricitinib, especially in severe cases, require treatment for a long duration. Androgenetic alopecia Androgen synthesis and metabolism: The effect of testosterone on hair growth is mediated by its more potent metabolite 5α dihydrotestosterone (DHT). The conversion of testosterone to DHT is catalyzed by the enzyme 5α‐reductase. There are three isoforms of 5α‐reductase, which are encoded by different genes . Type 1 5α‐reductase is widely distributed in the skin. The specificity of the response of hair follicles to androgens is determined within the skin. Hair follicles in occipital skin, a site that shows little or no response to androgens, retain their site‐specific behaviour when transplanted into balding areas on the frontal scalp . Conversely, hair follicles from a balding scalp continue to regress when transplanted into skin of the forearm Androgenetic alopecia Characterized by a progressive decline in hair fiber production by scalp hair follicles and their eventual miniaturization. As the pattern of hair loss differs between men and women, the terms male pattern hair loss and female pattern hair loss are also used. Deep frontal recession and/or vertex balding may also start shortly after puberty although in most men the onset is later. Hair loss progresses to a bald scalp in 50–60% of men by the age of 70 years. A small proportion of men (15–20%) do not show balding. Female pattern hair loss, 3–6% in women aged under 30 years, increasing to 29–42% in women aged 70 and over. Associated diseases Scalp pain. Prostate cancer. FPHL is associated with hyperaldosteronism, hypertension , hyperandrogenism and polycystic ovary disease, elevated cholesterol and an increased risk of late onset diabetes. Pathogensis The dermal papilla is central to the maintenance and control of hair growth and is likely to be the target of androgen‐mediated events leading to follicle miniaturization and hair cycle changes. In AGA, the duration of anagen decreases with each successive cycle, whereas the length of telogen remains constant or is pro longed. Pathogensis Ultimately, anagen duration becomes so short that the growing hair fails to achieve sufficient length to reach the surface of the skin, leaving an empty follicular pore. There is a gradual diminution in the size of follicles that results from the transformation of terminal follicles into vellus‐type follicles. Hair follicle miniaturization leads to finer hair that is often lighter in colour. Pathogensis The diffuse hair loss pattern seen in FPHL is due to a reduction in the number of terminal hairs per follicular unit rather than miniaturization of entire follicular units. Baldness occurs only when all the hairs within the follicular units are miniaturized and is a relatively early event in men and a late event in women. Genetic factor: risk increases with the number of affected family members, and the high frequency of baldness in the fathers of balding men. Differential diagnosis The principal differential diagnosis of early FPHL is chronic telogen effluvium (CTE) . Women with CTE present with chronic diffuse hair shedding without noticeable widening of the central parting. Alopecia Areata Incognita and Systemic Lupus Erythematosus. Treatment Minoxidil lotion: ( 2% in women, 5% in men) Minoxidil is a piperidinopyrimidine derivative and a potent vasodilator that is effective orally for severe hypertension. When applied topically in a lotion or foam vehicle, minoxidil increased terminal hair density in up to 30% of individuals . Finasteride: (1 mg/day ) Finasteride is a synthetic steroid that is a potent and selective antagonist of 5α‐reductase type 2, which inhibits the conversion of testosterone to DHT. Treatment Anti androgens: Only in females. Spironolactone . Cyproterone acetate. Flutamide. Hair transplantation. Acquired cicatricial alopecia Cicatricial alopecia refers to patchy hair loss that follows the permanent destruction of hair follicles, either by a disease affect ing the follicles themselves (primary cicatricial alopecia) or by an external process (secondary cicatricial alopecia). Discoid lupus erythematosus (Chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus) Lupus erythematosus is an autoimmune, connective tissue dis ease characterized by the presence of circulating non‐organ‐spe cific autoantibodies to cell nuclear antigens . Three different forms are described: systemic lupus erythemato sus (SLE), subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SCLE) and chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus (CCLE). However, only CCLE regularly produces cicatricial alopecia. Clinical features Scarring alopecia occurs in 20% of men and 50% of women affected with CCLE, and the scalp is the only area affected in a significant number of patients. Areas of erythema and scaling with follicular plugging extend irregularly across the scalp and produce scarring . Symptoms may include pruritus, burning or scalp tenderness. Pigmentary disturbance, particularly in dark‐skinned people, is common. Squamous cell carcinoma has been reported in chronic cicatricial lupus erythematosus of the scalp. Investigations Antinuclear antibody (ANA) is positive in approximately 35% of patients with CCLE. Anti‐Ro antibodies are found in 10%. Skin biopsy. Prognosis CCLE may occur on its own or associated with SLE. If the initial CCLE is confined to the head and neck, the risk is 1–2%, whereas if the lesions are generalized the risk is 22%. SLE first presents with CCLE in 10% of cases and CCLE can be found at some stage during the course of SLE in 33%. Differential diagnosis Causes of cicatrical alopecia: Inflammatory types of tinea capitis . Tertiary stage of syphilis. Lichenplano pilaris. Deep infections and deep trauma. Folliculitis decalvans Scleroderma. Treatment: Potent topical corticosteroids, Intralesional triamcinolone and Systemic prednisolone (1 mg/kg) may halt the progression of active CCLE. Antimalarials: hydroxychloroquine in a regimen of 200–400 mg/day. Others: Dapsone, thalidomide, vitamin E, oral gold, clofazamine, topical pimecrolimus, Cyclophosphamide, methotrexate. text: Leukodermas ( hypomelanosis ) Vitiligo Vitiligo is a common form of localized depigmentation. It is an acquired condition resulting from the progressive loss of melanocytes. It is characterized by milky‐white sharply demarcated macules. Types: non‐segmental forms of vitiligo (including several variants: acrofacial, mucosal, generalized, uni versal, mixed and rare variants of vitiligo) . Segmental vitiligo (uni‐, bi‐, or plurisegmental). Vitiligo It is stated that vitiligo affects 0.5–1% of the world’s population. Vitiligo can begin at any age but in the majority of cases becomes apparent between the age of 20 and 30 years. The prevalence is most probably the same in both sexes. Vitiligo affects all races. Associated conditions Pathophysiology Histochemical studies show a lack of dopa‐positive melanocytes in the basal layer of the epidermis . Electron microscopy studies confirm the loss of melanocytes. Various theories have been suggested for the aetiology of vitiligo; the same mechanism may not apply to all cases. Moreover, the loss of melanocytes in vitiligo may also be the result of different pathogenetic mechanisms working together (‘convergence’ or ‘integrated’ theory). The autoimmune/autoinflammatory theory It is based on the clinical association of vitiligo with a number of disorders also considered to be autoimmune or autoinflammatory . Several components of the innate immune system have been found to be associated with vitiligo . Antibodies to normal human melanocytes have been detected using a specific immunoprecipitation assay. A major etiological role for melanocyte‐specific cytotoxic T cells in coordinating the targeted autoimmune tissue destruction of melanocytes in progressive vitiligo . Oxidative theory Increased oxidative stress play an important role in in the formation of highly immunogenic neoantigens in vitiligo. Genetic theory A genetic factor is undoubtedly involved in vitiligo. Inheritance has been suggested to be polygenic. Approximately 30% of patients have a positive family history and vitiligo has been reported in monozygotic twins. Neural theory Neurogenic mechanism has been suggested whereby it has been hypothesized that a com pound released at peripheral nerve endings in the skin could have a toxic effect on melanocytes. Strassner JP, Harris JE. Understanding mechanisms of autoimmunity through translational research in vitiligo. Curr Opin Immunol. 2016;443:81–8. Koebner phenomenon It has been defined as the development of lesions at sites of trauma to uninvolved skin of patients with cutaneous diseases . Le Poole C, Boissy RE. Vitiligo. Semin Cutan Med Surg. 1997;16:3–14. Clinical types Non segmental type: The amelanotic macules in vitiligo are found particularly in areas of repeated friction, chonic pressure or trauma, for example the hips, dorsa of the hands/fingers, feet, elbows, knees and ankles . Bilateral, symmetrical. Prone to sunburn. Segmental type it is usually unilateral and band shaped ( mostly in children). Complete vitiligo (universalis), although most often a few pigmented areas remain indefinitely. The pigment loss may be partial or complete, or both may occur in the same areas (trichrome vitiligo). (poliosis/leukotrichia) may be present. The main symptom is the cosmetic disability, although some patients present because of sunburn in the amelanotic areas. Mixed vitiligo: the coexistence of non‐segmental and segmental vitiligo in one patient. Hypochromic vitiligo : partial defect in pigmentation. Inflammatory vitiligo Erythema at the margin of a vitiligo macule is referred to as “vitiligo with raised inflammatory borders” or inflammatory vitiligo. 21 Special types: Drug induces vitiligo: ex, clofazimine, chloroquine. Chemical induced leukodermas: ex, phenolic compounds, sulfahydryl, arsenic, corticosteroids, azaleic acid and mercury. Vitiligo with melanoma/ halo nevus: Perilesional or Diffuse hypopigmentation or depigmentation. Investigations Inspection with the aid of a Wood’s light can then be helpful. Ophthalmological examination. CBC. Thyroid function. Fasting blood glucose. Skin biopsy: in hypopigmented lesions. Histopathology In lesions of vitiligo, melanocytes are typically absent or present in very small numbers . The epidermal melanocyte density can be assessed with melanocyte-specific immunohistochemical stains, such as Melan-A (MART-1), MITF, and HMB45. Differential diagnosis Halo naevi. Naevus depigmentosus. Naevus anaemicus Inherited or genetically induced hypomelanosis (usually pre sent at birth). Post‐infectious hypomelanosis (e.g. pityriasis versicolor, leprosy). Piebaldism. Waardenburg syndrome. Tuberous sclerosis Pigmentary mosaicism (hypomelanosis of Ito). Progressive macular hypomelanosis. Secondary hypomelanosis (Post‐inflammatory hypomelanosis e.g. pityriasis alba, lichen sclerosus, morphoea) . Post‐traumatic hypomelanosis. Treatment Response to treatment of vitiligo varies between individuals but is often unsatisfactory, especially for acral lesions. Cosmetic camouflage can be used in some cases. First line: Topical corticosteroids: once‐daily application of potent topical corticosteroid preparations is effective at inducing repigmentation of areas of vitiligo. It is preferable to use an intermittent regimen (e.g. 15 days per month for 6 months) to avoid local side effects (skin atrophy, telangiectasia, striae, hypertrichosis and acneform eruptions). Topical calcineurin inhibitors: Use of topical calcineurin inhibitors (pimecrolimus, tacrolimus) has been reported to be successful, mainly for lesions on the face and neck: twice‐daily applications are recommended, initially for 6 months. Topical JAK inhibitors: Is used for non segmental vitiligo.( Ruxolitinib) it is janus kinase inhibitor aim to reduce the autoimmune response that leads to melanocyte destruction. It is applied twice daily to affected areas of upto 10% of the body. Second line: Phototherapy Narrow‐band UVB: (311–313 nm) Thrice‐weekly NB‐UVB has been shown to clear psoriasis more quickly. The initial dose is based on skin phototesting and the determination of the minimal erythemal dose (MED) or on skin phototype. Due to concerns regarding increased risk of SCC, the scrotum and genital skin should be protected from irradiation. NB‐UVB causes cutaneous immunomodulation partly by increasing vitamin D and similar to PUVA induces apoptosis of T cells and reduces epidermal hyperproliferation. PUVA photochemotherapy The combination of psoralens and long‐wave ultraviolet radiation (UVA 320–400 nm). The psoralens that are commonly used are 8‐methoxypsoralen (8‐MOP), 5‐methoxypsoralen (5‐MOP) and trioxypsoralen (T‐MOP). Psoralens are used either topically or orally in combination with UVA. This modality is highly efficacious in treating psoriasis with reported clearance rates of over 90%. Excimer laser and lamp The operational wavelength of the 308 nm excimer laser and lamp is close to that of NB-UVB . These surgical techniques are based on a common basic principle: to trans plant autologous melanocytes from a normal pigmented area to the affected depigmented skin. Different surgical techniques for repigmenting vitiligo include tis sue grafts (full‐thickness punch grafts, split‐thickness grafts, suction blister grafts) and cellular grafts (cultured melanocytes, cultured epithelial sheet grafts and non‐cultured epidermal cellular grafts) and hair follicle outer root sheath cells. text: Skin in systemic disease 1 skin in systemic disease SLOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Assess a patient presenting with pruritus, recognising potential systemic causes and ordering the appropriate investigations 2. Describe cutaneous manifestations of underlying systemic disease: a) Clinical features of Vitamin A, C, K, B, b) Enumerate important cutaneous signs of Paraneoplastic phenomena c) Recognise typical nail changes seen in common dermatoses and those associated with systemic disease 2 Pruritus Pruritus can be defined as an unpleasant sensation that elicits a desire to scratch. Pruritus is the most common skin-related symptom. It often arises from a primary cutaneous disorder but can be a manifestation of an underlying systemic disease in 15%–50% of affected individuals, especially when generalized. Non-dermatologic conditions that can lead to generalized pruritus include: Hepatic dysfunction, Primary biliary cholangitis ( in 80% of patients, often the presenting symptom), Hepatitis C viral infection (~15%) renal dysfunction, End-stage kidney disease on hemodialysis ( in 25-30% of patients) thyroid dysfunction; diabetes, lymphoma(Hodgkin lymphoma ≤30%, Non-Hodgkin lymphoma ≤10%), myeloproliferative neoplasms (e.g. polycythemia vera 30%–50%), and chronic lymphocytic leukemia (<5%) HIV neuropsychiatric disorders . Cutaneous T cell lymphoma 60%–80% overall; >90% in Sézary syndrome Pregnancy ~20% 4 Laboratory and radiographic evaluation in patients with pruritus of unknown etiology 5 Laboratory and radiographic evaluation in patients with pruritus of unknown etiology Basic initial evaluation • Complete blood count (CBC) with differential • Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP) • Creatinine, blood urea nitrogen (BUN) • Liver transaminases, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin • Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) • Thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) • Fasting plasma glucose • Serum ferritin, serum iron, and total iron binding capacity Possible additional evaluation • Skin biopsy Serum total and/or allergen-specific IgE Serum protein electrophoresis, serum immunofixation electrophoresis Viral hepatitis panel (including hepatitis B and C viruses); HIV testing Parathyroid function (calcium, phosphate, parathyroid hormone levels) Serum tryptase Stool for ova/parasites 6 Laboratory and radiographic evaluation in patients with pruritus of unknown etiology Radiographic studies • Chest X-ray or CT scan • Abdominal and pelvic ultrasonography or CT scan • Lymph node ultrasonography • Spinal X-ray or MRI (for regional pruritus) Other investigations • Age-appropriate cancer screening 7 Paraneoplastic phenomena Acquired hypertrichosis lanuginosa Growth of fine lanugo hairs in a generalized distribution or localized to the face. Associated with a variety of internal malignancies, most often carcinoma of the lung, colon, or breast Carcinoid syndrome Rosacea-like flushing and erythema of the head and neck and Pellagra-like dermatitis and sclerodermoid changes may develop in advanced disease Flushing associated with ~10% of mid-gut tumors (small intestine, appendix, proximal colon) with liver metastases; type III gastric and bronchial carcinoid tumors are also associated with flushing (liver metastases are not required) Paraneoplastic phenomena Paraneoplastic pemphigus Erosive disease of the mucous membranes and erythema multiforme-like, bullous pemphigoid-like or lichenoid skin lesions Most often associated with non-Hodgkin lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic leukemia or Castleman disease. Bronchiolitis obliterans is a common complication Acanthosis nigricans Rapid onset of hyperpigmented velvety changes in multiple flexural sites (e.g. neck, axillae, groin). May also involve extensor surfaces (e.g. elbows, knees, knuckles) and, in malignancy-associated cases, lips, oral mucosa, and palms (tripe palm). Associated with adenocarcinomas (e.g. stomach, other sites within the GI or GU tracts) and often accompanied by weight loss. Paraneoplastic phenomena Dermatomyositis (adult) Diffuse scaling and pruritus of the scalp, heliotrope rash, photodistributed poikiloderma, Gottron papules of the hands, thin plaques of the elbows, knees, lateral hips/thighs (holster sign) and upper back (shawl sign), nail-fold overgrowth with dilated capillary loops . Associated with ovarian, lung, colorectal, and pancreatic carcinomas and non-Hodgkin lymphoma Acquired ichthyosis Resembles ichthyosis vulgaris; most often located on the legs. Most commonly associated with lymphoma, which typically predates the diagnosis of the ichthyosis. Paraneoplastic phenomena Cutaneous small vessel vasculitis Palpable purpura; may be widespread and/or in unusual locations . text: Cutaneous Manifestations of HIV 1 SLOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to Recognize the cutaneous manifestations of the different stages of HIV Sample Footer Text 8/29/2025 2 Types and Pathogenesis of HIV, WHO Clinical Staging of HIV/AIDS 2 There are two types of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), HIV-1 and the less common HIV-2. Both are enveloped, single-stranded RNA lentiviruses in the Retroviridae family. Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infects human Th cells, leading to a progressive immunodeficiency disease, and causes acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). Cutaneous manifestations are prominent, affecting up to 90% of HIV-infected persons. In a person living with HIV, acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) is defined by a CD4+ cell count of <200/mm3 or <14% CD4+ T cells and/or the presence of an AIDS-defining condition. Sample Footer Text 8/29/2025 3 Figure 1: Replication of HIV within CD4+ lymphocyte and target sites of antiretroviral drugs (Dermatology, 5th Edition By Jean L. Bolognia, 2024) Sample Footer Text 8/29/2025 4 WHO clinical staging of HIV/AIDS in the setting of confirmed HIV infection: Clinical stage 1 – asymptomatic; immunologic correlate: ≥500 CD4+ cells/mm3 • Asymptomatic • Persistent generalized lymphadenopathy Clinical stage 2 – mild; immunologic correlate: 350–499 CD4+ cells/mm3 • Herpes zoster • Fungal nail infection • Pruritic papular eruptions • Angular cheilitis • Recurrent oral ulcerations • Recurrent/chronic upper respiratory tract infections (sinusitis, otitis media/ otorrhea, tonsillitis, pharyngitis) • Seborrheic dermatitis • Moderate unexplained weight loss (<10% of body weight) Sample Footer Text 8/29/2025 5 Clinical stage 3 – advanced; immunologic correlate: 200–349 CD4+ cells/mm3 • Persistent oral candidiasis • Oral hairy leukoplakia • Acute necrotizing ulcerative stomatitis, gingivitis, or periodontitis • Unexplained chronic diarrhea (>1 month in adults, >2 weeks in children) • Unexplained persistent fever (≥37.6°C intermittent or constant, for >1 month) • Pulmonary tuberculosis (current) • Unexplained anemia (<8g/dL), neutropenia (<0.5 × 109/L) or chronic thrombocytopenia (<50 × 109/L) • Unexplained severe weight loss (>10% of body weight) • Severe bacterial infections such as pneumonia, empyema, pyomyositis, bone or joint infection, meningitis, bacteremia Sample Footer Text 8/29/2025 6 Clinical stage 4 – severe/AIDS-defining conditions; immunologic correlate*: <200 CD4+ cells/mm3 • Chronic herpes simplex infection (orolabial, genital, or anorectal of >1 month’s duration or visceral at any site) • Kaposi sarcoma • Extrapulmonary cryptococcosis including meningitis • Disseminated endemic mycosis (coccidioidomycosis or histoplasmosis) • Disseminated non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection • Unexplained severe wasting, stunting or severe malnutrition not responding to standard therapy (HIV wasting syndrome) • Cytomegalovirus infection (retinitis or infection of other organs; onset at age >1 month) • HIV encephalopathy • Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy • Extrapulmonary tuberculosis • Candidiasis of the esophagus, trachea, bronchi, or lungs • Pneumocystis pneumonia • Central nervous system toxoplasmosis (onset at age >1 month) • Chronic cryptosporidiosis (with diarrhea)• Chronic isosporiasis • Symptomatic HIV-associated nephropathy or symptomatic HIV-associated cardiomyopathy • Cerebral or B cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma, or other HIV-associated solid tumor • Atypical disseminated leishmaniasis • Recurrent severe bacterial pneumonia • Recurrent non-typhoidal Salmonella bacteremia • Invasive cervical carcinoma Sample Footer Text 8/29/2025 7 Primary HIV exanthem (acute retroviral syndrome) Primary HIV infection refers to the initial disease phase, when HIV-1 RNA, DNA, and/or p24 antigen are present in the plasma prior to the development of HIV-1 antibodies. Initially, up to 80% of patients develop an “acute retroviral syndrome” resembling influenza or infectious mononucleosis. Symptoms develop 2–6 weeks after HIV exposure and often include fever, headache, myalgia/arthralgia, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, and night sweats. A morbilliform exanthem also occurs in 40%–80% of patients; it lasts 4–5 days and is typically generalized, with the most prominent involvement on the face and trunk. Oral and genital ulcers are occasionally present. Symptoms are self-limited and resolve in a few days to weeks, with a median duration of 14 days. The initial phase of rapid HIV-1 replication causes a temporary fall in CD4+ cell counts Sample Footer Text 8/29/2025 8 HIV-related infectious skin conditions Sample Footer Text 8/29/2025 9 As immunity wanes, the frequency of Herpes Simplex Virus recurrences increases and lesions take longer to heal, potentially evolving into chronic, extensive, deep, and painful ulcers that favor the perianal region, genitalia, and tongue. In people living with HIV, varicella tends to have new lesion formation over a longer period of time, a higher lesion count, and (particularly in adults) complications such as pneumonitis, hepatitis, and encephalitis. Lesions persist as slowly healing ulcers. Molluscum contagiosum (MC) commonly occurs and tends to be more persistent in individuals with significantly reduced CD4+ T cell counts. In addition to the typical presentation of small umbilicated papules , people living with HIV can develop larger (>1cm), coalescent, verrucous, and widespread lesions The prevalence of human papilloma virus (HPV) infection is higher in people living with HIV than in the general population and correlates with decreasing CD4+ T cell counts. People living with HIV have reduced HPV clearance, more treatment-resistant mucocutaneous lesions, and accelerated development of HPV-associated carcinoma. Skin lesions are often multiple, coalescent, and extensive Oral hairy leukoplakia (OHL) results from Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) infection of the oral mucosa and typically presents as hyperkeratotic, corrugated white plaques with hair-like projections on the lateral aspect of the tongue Sample Footer Text 8/29/2025 10 Reactivation of cytomegalovirus (CMV) is associated with CD4+ T cell counts that are <100/mm3, and it remains a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in patients with AIDS. Retinitis, esophagitis, and colitis represent common clinical manifestations, and mucosal ulcers may occur in the setting of disseminated disease. Cutaneous presentations are uncommon People living with HIV are at increased risk for the development of recurrent and potentially severe cutaneous bacterial infections, which can be localized or widespread and sometimes have unusual clinical appearances. A diverse clinical spectrum of tuberculous and non-tuberculous mycobacterial skin infections can develop in people living with HIV Rates of syphilis have risen over the past decade. In addition to classic papulosquamous lesions of secondary syphilis, people with HIV disease may present with lues maligna, also known as malignant or ulceronodular syphilis, which is a severe form of secondary Syphilis. Sample Footer Text 8/29/2025 11 Candidiasis is the most common fungal disease in those living with HIV, and its incidence and severity are both increased in the setting of lower CD4+ T cell counts. Oropharyngeal candidiasis is often the first clinical manifestation of HIV disease. Additional presentations include angular cheilitis, chronic paronychia, and onychodystrophy, as well as intertriginous, refractory vaginal, esophageal, and disseminated candidiasis. Individuals with HIV disease are predisposed to the development of disseminated cryptococcosis and dimorphic fungal infections, including histoplasmosis, blastomycosis, coccidioidomycosis, paracoccidioidomycosis, talaromycosis, emergomycosis, and sporotrichosis. Cryptococcus neoformans is an encapsulated yeast that is found worldwide in bird droppings and contaminated soil. Patients with CD4+ T cell counts <100/mm3 are particularly susceptible, and pulmonary or central nervous system disease may be the initial presentation of AIDS. Cutaneous lesions occur in 10%–20% of patients with disseminated cryptococcosis and often appear as molluscum contagiosum-like.
