text: Acne Vulgaris By the end of this lecture, students will be able to Describe the epidemiology, pathophysiology and common presentations of acne and acneiform eruptions. Describe treatment algorithm for comedonal, papulopustular, nodular acne. Recognize optimal use and adverse events of topical and systemic drugs for acne. Develop the ability to make differential diagnoses, by comparing and contrasting the features of acne vulgaris, rosacea, hidradenitis suppurativa. Sebaceous glands are almost always associated with hair follicles except for the free sebaceous glands found on the vermilion lips and oral mucosa (Fordyce spots or granules), eyelids (meibomian glands), areolae (Montgomery tubercles), and labia minora and prepuce (Tyson glands). Sebaceous glands produce sebum, which is released into the infundibular portion of the hair follicle. Sebum production increases at the time of puberty and is a critical factor in the pathogenesis of acne vulgaris. Acne affects ~85% of young people between 12 and 24 years of age. Nevertheless, preadolescent acne affects children 7 to 11 years of age and acne may continue into adulthood. The principal abnormality in acne is comedo formation. It is produced by the impaction and distention of the follicles with a keratinous plug in the lower infundibulum. The keratinous plug is caused by hyperproliferation and abnormal differentiation of keratinocytes. Androgens, alterations in lipid composition, and an abnormal response to local cytokines are all hypothesized to be important. As the retained cells block the follicular opening, the lower portion of the follicle is dilated by entrapped sebum. Disruption of the follicular epithelium permits discharge of the follicular contents into the dermis. The combination of keratin, sebum, and microorganisms, particularly Cutibacterium acnes, leads to the release of proinflammatory mediators and the accumulation of lymphocytes, neutrophils, and foreign body giant cells. This in turn causes the formation of inflammatory papules, pustules, and nodulocystic lesions Follicular Hyperkeratinization The microcomedo is thought to be the precursor of all clinically apparent acne lesions. Corneocytes, which are normally shed into the hair follicle lumen and extruded, accumulate due to increases in both follicular keratinocyte proliferation and corneocyte cohesiveness, leading to the development of a hyperkeratotic plug that acts as a bottle neck. Hormonal Influences on Sebum Production and Composition Sebum production is controlled primarily by androgens, with additional influences from other hormones and neuropeptides. Androgens are produced both outside the pilosebaceous unit, mainly by the gonads and adrenal glands, and locally within the sebaceous gland via the action of androgen-metabolizing enzymes such as 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (HSD), 17β-HSD and 5α-reductase. Androgen receptors, found in the cells of the basal layer of the sebaceous gland and the outer root sheath of the hair follicle, are responsive to testosterone and 5α-dihydrotestosterone (DHT), the most potent androgens. Inflammation in acne: It is clear that when a follicle involved with acne ruptures, it exudes keratin, sebum, C. acnes, and cellular debris into the surrounding dermis, thereby intensifying inflammation. Nevertheless, inflammation is also seen early in acne lesion formation. Cutibacterium acnes colonization and activities C. acnes is a Gram-positive, anaerobic/microaerophilic rod that is found on the skin surface and within the sebaceous follicle. Through activation of the TLR2 pathway, C. acnes stimulates the release of proinflammatory mediators such as IL-1α, IL-8, IL-12, tumor necrosis factor (TNF), and matrix metalloproteinases. IL-8 leads to neutrophil recruitment, the release of lysosomal enzymes, and subsequent disruption of the follicular epithelium, while IL-12 promotes Th1 responses. Dietary Factors The relationship between diet and acne remains controversial. Several observational studies have found that the intake of milk, especially skim milk, is positively associated with acne prevalence and severity. Exacerbation of acne with the use of whey protein supplements for body building has also been reported . Vitamin B12 supplementation can potentially trigger the development of acne or an acneiform eruption by altering the transcriptome of skin microbiota, leading to increased production of proinflammatory porphyrins by Cutibacterium acnes. Clinical Picture Acne is typically found in sites with well-developed sebaceous glands, most often the face and upper trunk. Acne lesions are divided into non-inflammatory and inflammatory groups based upon their clinical appearance. Non-inflammatory acne is characterized by open and closed comedones. Closed comedones (whiteheads) are generally small (~1 mm), skin-colored papules with no apparent follicular opening or associated erythema. Open comedones (blackheads) have a conspicuous dilated follicular opening that is filled with an inspissated core of shed keratin. Melanin deposition and lipid oxidation within the debris may be responsible for the black color. Inflammatory acne is characterized by papules, pustules, and nodules of varying severity. Erythematous papules typically range from 1 to 5 mm in diameter. Pustules tend to be approximately equal in size and are filled with white purulent material and normal microbiota, including C. acnes. As the severity of lesions progresses, nodules form and become markedly inflamed, indurated, and tender. The pseudocysts of acne are deeper and filled with a combination of pus and serosanguineous fluid. Acne Fulminans Acne fulminans is the most severe form of acne and is characterized by the abrupt development of nodular and suppurative acne lesions in association with systemic manifestations. This uncommon variant primarily affects boys 13–16 years of age. Osteolytic bone lesions may accompany the cutaneous findings. Systemic manifestations include fever, arthralgias, myalgias, hepatosplenomegaly, and severe malaise. Erythema nodosum may also arise in association with acne fulminans. Laboratory abnormalities include an elevated ESR, proteinuria, leukocytosis, and anemia, Recommended treatment of acne fulminans includes prednisone 0.5–1 mg/kg/day as monotherapy for at least 2–4 weeks, followed by initiation of low-dose isotretinoin (e.g. 0.1 mg/kg/day) after the acute inflammation subsides; after at least 4 weeks of this combination, the isotretinoin dose can be slowly increased and the prednisone tapered over a period of 1–2 months. Acne excoriée occurs more often in young women. Typical comedones and inflammatory papules are systematically excoriated in a ritualistic manner, leaving crusted erosions that may scar. Linear erosions suggest self-manipulation, and an underlying psychiatric component should be considered. Individuals with an anxiety, obsessive– compulsive, or body dysmorphic disorder are particularly at risk, and antidepressants or psychotherapy may be helpful in these patients. Drug induced acne: Acne or acneiform eruptions (e.g. folliculitis) can be seen as a side effect of a number of medications. An abrupt, monomorphous eruption of inflammatory papules and pustules is often observed in drug-induced acne, in contrast to the heterogeneous morphology of lesions seen in acne vulgaris. Examples of implicated drugs: anabolic steroids, bromides, EGFR inhibitors, iodides, JAK inhibitors, lithium, isoniazid, phenytoin, progestins, mTOR inhibitors. Occupational acne, acne cosmetica, and pomade acne: Exposure to insoluble, follicle-occluding substances in the workplace is responsible for occupational acne. Offending agents include cutting oils, petroleum-based products, chlorinated aromatic hydrocarbons, and coal tar derivatives. Comedones dominate the clinical picture, with varying numbers of papules, pustules, and cystic lesions distributed in exposed as well as typically covered areas. Primarily comedonal facial acne, with a predominance of closed comedones, can also develop in sites chronically exposed to follicle-occluding cosmetics (acne cosmetica) or hair products. The latter, referred to as pomade acne, favors the forehead and temples. Acne mechanica Acne mechanica is due to repeated mechanical and frictional obstruction of the pilosebaceous outlet. Comedo formation is the result. Mechanical factors include rubbing by helmets, chin straps, suspenders, and collars as well as friction between the inner thighs. Radiation acne is characterized by comedo-like papules occurring at sites of previous exposure to therapeutic ionizing radiation. The lesions begin to appear as the acute phase of radiation dermatitis starts to resolve. The ionizing rays induce epithelial metaplasia within the follicle, creating adherent hyperkeratotic plugs that are resistant to expression. Acne conglobate: A severe type of acne characterized by numerous comedones and large abscesses with interconnecting sinuses, cysts, and grouped inflammatory nodules. The cysts occur on the back, buttocks, chest, forehead, cheeks, anterior neck, and shoulders. The impact of androgens on sebaceous gland activity begins during the neonatal period. From birth until approximately 6–12 months of age, infant boys have elevated levels of luteinizing hormone (LH), which stimulates testicular production of testosterone. In addition, both male and female infants exhibit increased levels of dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) and DHEA sulphate (DHEAS) secondary to a large, androgen-producing “fetal zone” in the adrenal gland that involutes during the first year of life. Sebaceous gland activity in infants is not the result of persistent maternal hormonal stimulation, as was previously hypothesized. Both testicular and adrenal androgen production decrease substantially by 1 year of age and remain at a stable nadir until adrenarche. Differential Diagnosis • Acneiform eruptions • Rosacea • Hidradenitis suppurativa Treatment: Mild 1. Comedonal • Topical retinoid ± physical extraction (first line) • Alternate retinoid, salicylic acid, azelaic acid (second line) 2. Papular/pustular • Topical antimicrobial combination + topical retinoid, benzoyl peroxide wash if mild truncal lesions (first line) • Alternate antimicrobials + alternate topical retinoids, azelaic acid, sodium sulfacetamide–sulfur, salicylic acid (second line) Moderate Papular/pustular • Oral antibiotic + topical retinoid + benzoyl peroxide (first line) • Alternate antibiotic, alternate topical retinoid, alternate benzoyl peroxide (second line) • In women, spironolactone + oral contraceptive + topical retinoids ± topical antibiotic and/or benzoyl peroxide • Isotretinoin if relapses quickly off oral antibiotics, does not clear, or scars Severe Nodular/conglobate • Isotretinoin • Oral antibiotic + topical retinoid + benzoyl peroxide • In women, spironolactone + oral contraceptive + topical retinoid ± topical or oral antibiotics and/or benzoyl peroxide Topical retinoids: The anti-acne activity of topical retinoids involves normalization of follicular keratinization and corneocyte cohesion, which aids in the expulsion of existing comedones and prevents the formation of new ones. Topical retinoids also have significant anti-inflammatory properties. Topical retinoids used for acne include tretinoin, adapalene, tazarotene, and trifarotene Alternate-night to every-third-night application may be necessary initially, with increased frequency as tolerated. Because the standard generic tretinoin formulation is photolabile, night-time application is recommended. The most common side effect of topical retinoids is local irritation resulting in erythema, dryness, peeling, and scaling. This tends to peak after 2–4 weeks of treatment and improves with continued usage. Benzoyl peroxide is a potent bactericidal agent that reduces C. acnes within the follicle. It also has mild comedolytic properties. In contrast to topical antibiotics, microbial resistance to benzoyl peroxide has not been reported. As benzoyl peroxide is a bleaching agent, whitening of clothing and bedding can occur. Development of allergic contact dermatitis to benzoyl peroxide and its metabolite benzoic acid is also possible. Topical antibiotics: Topical formulations of clindamycin, erythromycin, and minocycline utilized for acne include creams, gels, foams, solutions, and pledgets. Azelaic acid: By inhibiting the growth of C. acnes, azelaic acid reduces inflammatory acne. It also reverses altered follicular keratinization and thus demonstrates some comedolytic properties. In addition, azelaic acid can help to lighten post inflammatory hyperpigmentation. Topical dapsone 5% and 7.5% gels are FDA-approved for the treatment of acne vulgaris in patients. Clascoterone 1% cream is a topical androgen receptor inhibitor that was recently approved for treatment of acne in patients ≥12 years of age. Systemic therapies First-line therapy for moderate to severe inflammatory acne includes use of oral tetracyclines, primarily doxycycline, minocycline, or sarecycline. Oral antibiotics should not be administered as monotherapy. Oral macrolide antibiotics, erythromycin and azithromycin, can be used for acne in patients who are unable to tolerate tetracyclines, pregnant, or <8 years of age. Hormonal therapy can be an effective acne treatment for female patients, irrespective of their serum androgen levels. Combined oral contraceptive pills, which contain an estrogen (usually ethinyl estradiol) plus a progestin, block both ovarian and adrenal production of androgens. Side effects from oral contraceptives include nausea, vomiting, abnormal menses, weight gain, and breast tenderness and rarely, hypertension and thromboembolism (e.g. deep venous thrombosis, pulmonary embolism). Spironolactone functions as an androgen receptor blocker and, in doses of 50–100 mg twice daily, has been shown to reduce sebum production and improve acne. Spironolactone side effects are dose-related and include irregular menstrual periods, breast tenderness, headache, and fatigue. Hyperkalemia is rare. Standard isotretinoin dosing for acne is 0.5–1 mg/kg/day taken with a fatty meal to increase gastrointestinal absorption. The most common adverse effects of isotretinoin involve the skin and mucous membranes and are dose-dependent. These include cheilitis, dryness of the oral and nasal mucosa, generalized xerosis, and skin fragility. Other cutaneous side effects such as excessive granulation tissue, paronychia, and cutaneous infections (in particular with Staphylococcus aureus) can also occur. Teratogenicity is a serious potential complication, and female patients of childbearing potential must have at least one negative pregnancy test(s) before starting treatment and practice effective contraception for 1 month prior to, during, and for 1 month after completing therapy. Isotretinoin therapy increases serum triglyceride and/or cholesterol levels in ~20%–50% of patients. Elevated serum creatine kinase levels and rhabdomyolysis have been reported \and are more common in athletes. Other potential side effects involve the musculoskeletal system (myalgias, low back pain), eyes, liver (occasional mild elevation in transaminases), and central nervous system. Surgical treatment Comedo extraction Intralesional injection of corticosteroid (triamcinolone acetonide can quickly improve the appearance and tenderness of deep, inflamed nodules and cysts. Low-concentration chemical peels are also beneficial for the reduction of comedones. Laser resurfacing (fractionated as well as traditional), dermabrasion, and deeper chemical peels seek to reduce depressed scars. Surgical subcision is also used for management of acne scars and punch grafting is an option for patients with scarring. Rosacea Rosacea usually develops in patients over the age of 30. The term “rosacea” encompasses a constellation of clinical findings, with either fixed centrofacial erythema in a characteristic pattern that may periodically intensify or phymatous changes classified as diagnostic features. Other common features are papules and pustules, flushing, telangiectasia, and ocular manifestations such as blepharitis and chalazia. The exact etiology of rosacea is not clear, but the following factors are probably involved: • Innate immune system dysregulation • Neurovascular dysregulation • Genetic predisposition • Hypersensitivity to certain mites that live near hair follicles (called Demodex mites) or bacteria Possible triggers of rosacea flare-ups include sunlight, extreme heat or cold, and stress. Avoid triggers ; alcohol, hot drinks, medications, hot spices and spicy foods, sunlight, extreme temperatures. • Brimonidine is effective against erythema • Topical azelaic acid, ivermectin or metronidazole help to reduce nodules and pimples. • Topical clindamycin, benzoyl peroxide, pimedrolimus or tacraolimus • Anti-inflammatory antibiotic doxycycline. • Isotretinoin given in lower doses than in acne vulgaris (0.3 mg/kg), and at times as a long-term suppressant, may be necessary for management of more resistant disease. • Nose-related symptoms (rhinophyma) can be treated with oral medication or surgical approaches to the reshaping of rhinophyma (of a heated scalpel, electrocautery, dermabrasion, laser ablation, tangential excision combined with scissors sculpting, and radiofrequency electrosurgery). Hidradenitis suppuritava Hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is a chronic cutaneous disorder that preferentially affects intertriginous skin, in particular the axillae and anogenital regions. It is characterized by recurrent inflammatory nodules and abscesses that may progress to form draining sinus tracts and scars HS is a multifactorial inflammatory disease that is a consequence of follicular occlusion and immune dysregulation and is influenced by genetics/ epigenetics, the cutaneous microbiome, and hormones. Clinical picture Typical lesions include comedones (including double-ended comedones; , inflammatory papules and nodules, abscesses, tunnels (both sinus tracts and skin fistulae), and scars. Lesions favour major body folds including the axillae, groin, buttocks, and inframammary areas. Occasionally, the face, post-auricular region, neck, and trunk are involved. Initially, patients have recurrent inflammatory papulonodules and abscesses that are tender and extremely painful. Over time, tunnels and scars may develop. This can be accompanied by chronic, malodorous drainage, leading to a marked degree of frustration, embarrassment, and self-consciousness. The discharged fluid is often a mixture of serous exudate, blood and pus, in varying proportions. Complications include soft tissue infections, lymphedema, and scarring so severe as to lead to strictures of the urethra, anus, and rectum as well as limb contractures. Rarely, squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) arises within chronic HS lesions. Treatment General measures • Pain management, smoking cessation, and a healthy diet • If obese or overweight, weight reduction is recommended • Recommend wearing soft, breathable fabrics and loose undergarments to reduce friction and moisture • Recommend antiseptic soaps, e.g. benzoyl peroxide or chlorhexidine washes • Provide and educate patient on wound care • Consider laser hair reduction Mild disease • Intralesional triamcinolone injections into inflamed lesions • Topical therapies: resorcinol, clindamycin, dapsone • Oral antibiotics: tetracyclines (doxycycline, minocycline), clindamycin, rifampin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, metronidazole, moxifloxacin • Hormonal therapies: spironolactone, oral contraceptive pills with antiandrogenic or low androgenic progestins, metformin, finasteride. • Oral retinoids (especially if patient also has cystic acne): acitretin, isotretinoin • Complementary and alternative medicine: oral zinc • Surgical treatments; deroofing, limited local excisions Moderate disease • Medical therapies for mild disease, alone or in combination with the following: • Systemic immunomodulators (“biologics”): TNF inhibitors (adalimumab, infliximab), ustekinumab, IL-17 inhibitors, IL-23 inhibitors, IL-1 antagonists. • Other systemic immunomodulators/immunosuppressants: apremilast, colchicine (in combination with minocycline), cyclosporine, corticosteroids • Surgical treatments; deroofing, local excisions, Nd:YAG laser, CO2 laser ablation Severe disease • Medical treatments outlined for mild and moderate disease, alone or in combination with the following: • Intravenous antibiotics: ertapenem • Surgical treatments; deroofing, wide surgical excision of involved areas, CO2 laser excision

name: PPT: eczema
text: Eczematous Eruptions What is Eczema? Definition: Eczema, from the Greek ekzein ("to boil forth"), is a pattern of inflammatory skin reaction, not a single disease. Clinical Features: Acute: Red, swollen (edematous) plaques, sometimes with tiny grouped vesicles (blisters). Subacute: Red plaques with scale or crusting. Chronic: Dry scale or lichenification (thickened skin with prominent skin lines from chronic rubbing). Key Symptom: Severe pruritus (itching) is a prominent feature, often worse at night and exacerbated by heat, sweat, and stress. Histology: The hallmark of all eczematous reactions is spongiosis—serous fluid between epidermal cells—with a perivascular infiltrate of lymphocytes. Atopic Dermatitis (AD) - The "Itch that Rashes" Definition: A chronic, inflammatory, and intensely pruritic skin disease with a course of exacerbations and remissions. It's often the first step in the "atopic march," preceding food allergies, asthma, and allergic rhinitis. Itching often begins before the rash appears Epidemiology of AD Prevalence: A major global health issue, with prevalence dramatically increasing in the latter half of the 20th century. Rates are up to 30% in developed nations and exceed 10% in many other countries. Worldwide cumulative prevalence is around 20%. Risk Factors: Geography: High latitude and lower mean annual temperature. Genetics: A strong genetic link exists. If both parents are atopic, the risk for a child developing allergic symptoms is ~79%. Birth/Early Life: Cesarean delivery, first-born status, antibiotic exposure prenatally, and a "Western diet" alter the gut microbiome and increase risk. Pathophysiology of AD - A "Barrier-First" Disease AD is a vicious cycle of a defective skin barrier and immune dysregulation. Barrier Defect: Genetic: Null mutations in the Filaggrin gene (FLG) are a major factor. Filaggrin is essential for creating the "natural moisturizing factor" (NMF) that keeps skin hydrated. Reduced NMF leads to xerosis (dry skin) and increased transepidermal water loss (TEWL). A compromised barrier allows allergens and microbes to penetrate the skin more easily. Immune Dysregulation: The barrier breach triggers a T-helper 2 (Th2) dominant immune response. Keratinocytes release cytokines, which promotes Th2 inflammation. Th2 cells release key cytokines: IL-4 and IL-13: Drive the inflammatory feedback loop and further impair the barrier. IL-31: Binds directly to nerves, causing intense itch, and also downregulates filaggrin expression. Clinical Presentation of AD - Age-Specific Patterns Infantile AD (2 months - 2 years): Begins as red, scaly patches, often on the cheeks. Can spread to the scalp, forehead, and extensor surfaces of arms and legs. Lesions are often exudative ("weepy") and crusted. Childhood AD (2 - 10 years): Classic "flexural" distribution: antecubital (elbow creases) and popliteal (knee creases) fossae. Also affects the face, neck, wrists, and ankles. Lesions are typically less weepy and more lichenified (thickened) from chronic scratching. Adolescent/Adult AD: Often involves flexural areas, neck, forehead, and around the eyes. Lichenification and prurigo-like (intensely itchy, firm) papules are common. Can present as localized eczema, especially on the hands, eyelids, or nipples. Diagnostic Criteria for AD (Hanifin & Rajka) Diagnosis is clinical. No lab test is diagnostic. Criteria are used mainly for research but are helpful clinically. Must have 3 of 4 MAJOR criteria: Pruritus (itching). Typical morphology and distribution (flexural for adults, facial/extensor for infants). Chronic or chronically relapsing dermatitis. Personal or family history of atopy (asthma, allergic rhinitis, AD). Must ALSO have 3 or more MINOR criteria: Xerosis (dry skin). Ichthyosis / Hyperlinear palms / Keratosis pilaris. Elevated serum IgE. Early age of onset. Tendency for skin infections (e.g., Staphylococcus aureus). Nipple eczema. Dennie-Morgan infraorbital fold (fold under the lower eyelid). Main Management Lines: The Stepped-Care Approach Management is multifaceted, focusing on barrier repair, inflammation control, and trigger avoidance. Foundation of Care: Barrier Repair & Education: Moisturize! This is the cornerstone of AD care. Use thick, bland emollients (e.g., petrolatum-based) daily, especially after bathing ("soak and smear"). Gentle Cleansing: Use lukewarm water, limit soap, and choose non-soap, pH-balanced cleansers. Education: A written action plan is crucial for patient/parent understanding and adherence. Controlling Inflammation: Anti-inflammatory Topicals: Topical Corticosteroids: First-line for flares. Potency is matched to body site and severity. Ointments are preferred. Topical Calcineurin Inhibitors (TCIs): Tacrolimus, Pimecrolimus. Excellent for sensitive areas (face, eyelids) and for maintenance therapy to prevent flares. Topical PDE4 Inhibitors: Crisaborole. A non-steroidal option for mild-to-moderate AD. Main Management Lines Managing Itch & Infection: Antipruritics: Sedating antihistamines (e.g., hydroxyzine) can help with sleep. Antimicrobials: Secondary bacterial infection (S. aureus) is common and causes flares. Dilute bleach baths (e.g., ¼ cup in a full bathtub) twice weekly can reduce bacterial colonization and inflammation. Topical or oral antibiotics may be needed for active infection. Advanced Therapies for Severe/Refractory AD: Phototherapy: Narrow-band UVB (NB-UVB) is highly effective. Systemic Therapies: Biologics: Dupilumab (injectable IL-4/IL-13 receptor inhibitor) is a targeted therapy that significantly reduces itch and rash. Immunosuppressants: Cyclosporine, methotrexate, azathioprine, and others may be used for severe cases. Systemic corticosteroids should be avoided for long-term use due to side effects and rebound flares Common Eczematous Eruptions: Regional Eczemas Localized eczema can be a manifestation of AD, contact dermatitis (allergic/irritant), or other conditions. Ear Eczema (Otitis Externa): Affects the external auditory canal, helix, or postauricular fold. Often a sign of seborrheic dermatitis or allergic contact dermatitis (e.g., to neomycin in ear drops, nickel in earrings). Secondary bacterial infection is common. Eyelid Dermatitis: Most often related to AD or allergic contact dermatitis. Common allergens include fragrances, preservatives in cosmetics/eye drops, metals (nickel), and nail polish (transferred by hands). Management requires identifying and eliminating triggers; patch testing is recommended. Breast (Nipple) Eczema: Affects the areolae, often with oozing, crusting, and painful fissuring. Can be the sole manifestation of AD in adult women, especially during breastfeeding. Important: Unilateral nipple eczema persisting >3 months requires a biopsy to rule out Paget disease of the breast. Hand Eczema: Hand Eczema: Very common, especially in atopic individuals and certain occupations ("wet work" like healthcare, hairdressing). Can be irritant, allergic, or atopic in origin. Presents in various forms: vesicular ("dyshidrosis"), hyperkeratotic (thickened, fissured), or affecting fingertips (pulpitis). Diaper (Napkin) Dermatitis: An irritant dermatitis from prolonged contact with urine and feces, leading to maceration and skin breakdown. Clinical Pearl: Typically spares the skin folds, unlike candidiasis or inverse psoriasis. Prevention is key: frequent diaper changes and use of superabsorbent diapers and barrier creams (zinc oxide, petrolatum). Circumstomal Eczema: Eczema around an ileostomy or colostomy site, very common post-operatively. Caused by leakage of irritating intestinal fluid onto the skin. Treatment involves barrier powders or pastes and topical steroids, but application can be tricky due to poor appliance adherence. Eczematous Eruptions in Specific Populations Xerotic Eczema: "Winter itch" seen in elderly individuals or during dry winter months. Dehydrated skin develops fine cracks, resembling "cracked porcelain," on shins, arms, and flanks. Caused by an impaired epidermal barrier and increased TEWL. Pruritic Dermatitis in the Elderly: Common, often eczematous or papular, and may resemble nummular eczema or insect bites (subacute prurigo). Pathogenesis may be related to age-related barrier failure and immune changes (skewing toward a Th2 response). Treatment is similar to AD: emollients, topical steroids, and phototherapy for refractory cases. Hormonal Dermatoses: Autoimmune Progesterone Dermatitis: A rare, cyclical eruption (eczematous, urticarial, or targetoid lesions) that appears 5-7 days before menses and resolves after. Autoimmune Estrogen Dermatitis: Similar cyclical pattern but exacerbated premenstrually. References Andrews’ Diseases of the Skin Clinical Dermatology, THIRTEENTH EDITION

name: PPT: bullous dermatoses
text: Bullous Dermatoses SLOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to Describe the pathogenesis (pemphigus, bullous pemphigoid, dermatitis herpetiformis) Differentiate and describe lesions starting from clinical cases. Describe the histopathology, enumerate investigations. Explain the main treatments including biologics. Pemphigus is a group of autoimmune blistering diseases of the skin and mucous membranes that is characterized by: histologically, intraepidermal blisters due to the loss of cell–cell adhesion of keratinocytes, immunopathologically the finding of in vivo bound and circulating IgG autoantibodies directed against the cell surface of keratinocytes. Clinical types Two main types; Pemphigus vulgaris and pemphigus foliaceus. Pemphigus vegetans is a variant of pemphigus vulgaris, and pemphigus erythematosus and fogo selvagem represent localized and endemic variants of pemphigus foliaceus, respectively. Autoantibodies are directed against the cell surface of keratinocytes, resulting in the loss of cell–cell adhesion of keratinocytes through a process called acantholysis. The functional inhibition of desmogleins, which play an important role in cell–cell adhesion of keratinocytes, by IgG autoantibodies results in blister formation. Patients with pemphigus vulgaris and pemphigus foliaceus have IgG autoantibodies against desmoglein 3 and desmoglein 1, respectively. The mean age of onset of disease is 50 to 60 years, although the range is broad and disease arising in the elderly and in children has been described. Mucous membrane lesions usually present as painful erosions. Intact blisters are rare, in the oral cavity, the most common sites are the buccal and palatine mucosae. The erosions are painful, may result in decreased oral intake of food or liquids. Involvement of the throat produces hoarseness and difficulty in swallowing. The oesophagus also may be involved and sloughing of its entire lining in the form of a cast has been reported. The conjunctivae, nasal mucosa, vagina, labia, penis and anus can develop lesions as well. The primary skin lesions of pemphigus vulgaris are flaccid, thin walled, easily ruptured blisters. They can appear anywhere on the skin surface and arise on either normal- appearing skin or erythematous bases. The blisters are fragile and soon rupture to form painful erosions that ooze and bleed easily. These erosions often attain a large size and can become generalized. The erosions soon become partially covered with crusts. Because of an absence of cohesion within the epidermis, its upper layers easily move laterally with slight pressure or rubbing in patients with active disease (Nikolsky sign). The lack of cohesion of the skin may also be demonstrated with the “bulla-spread phenomenon” – gentle pressure on an intact bulla forces the fluid to spread under the skin away from the site of pressure (Asboe–Hansen sign). Pemphigus vegetans is a rare vegetative variant of pemphigus vulgaris. Pemphigus vegetans is characterized by flaccid blisters that become erosions and then form fungoid vegetations or papillomatous proliferations. Pemphigus Foliaceus Patients with pemphigus foliaceus develop scaly, crusted cutaneous erosions, often on an erythematous base, but they do not have clinically apparent mucosal involvement even with widespread disease. Pemphigus erythematosus is simply a localized variant of pemphigus foliaceus. Typical scaly and crusted lesions of pemphigus foliaceus appear in “seborrheic” areas. In pemphigus vegetans, suprabasilar acantholysis is seen, in addition to considerable papillomatosis and acanthosis. In pemphigus foliaceus, there is acantholysis in the upper epidermis, within or adjacent to the granular layer (subcorneal intragranular). The dermis shows a moderate number of inflammatory cells. Histopathologic examination In pemphigus vulgaris the characteristic histologic finding in this form of pemphigus is intraepidermal blister formation due to a loss of cell–cell adhesion of keratinocytes (acantholysis). Acantholysis occurs just above the basal cell layer (suprabasilar acantholysis). A few rounded-up (acantholytic) keratinocytes are often seen within the blister cavity. Although the basal cells lose lateral desmosomal contact with their neighbors, they maintain their attachment to the basement membrane via hemidesmosomes, thus giving the appearance of a “row of tombstones” the dermis there is a moderate perivascular mononuclear cell infiltrateHistopathologic examination In pemphigus vulgaris the characteristic histologic finding in this form of pemphigus is intraepidermal blister formation due to a loss of cell–cell adhesion of keratinocytes (acantholysis). Acantholysis occurs just above the basal cell layer (suprabasilar acantholysis). A few rounded-up (acantholytic) keratinocytes are often seen within the blister cavity. Although the basal cells lose lateral desmosomal contact with their neighbors, they maintain their attachment to the basement membrane via hemidesmosomes, thus giving the appearance of a “row of tombstones” the dermis there is a moderate perivascular mononuclear cell infiltrate Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) examines patients’ skin or mucous membranes in order to demonstrate in vivo bound IgG deposition on the keratinocyte cell surfaces (honey-comb appearance). DIF is the most reliable and sensitive diagnostic test for all forms of pemphigus. ELISA is increasingly being used to detect antigen-specific autoantibodies for the diagnosis of pemphigus. The patient’s serum is tested on ELISA plates pre-coated with relevant recombinant proteins, e.g. Dsg1, Dsg3. Thus, specific antibodies directed against desmogleins can be detected. Indirect immunofluorescence (IIF) examines patients’ sera in order to demonstrate circulating IgG autoantibodies directed against epithelial cell surfaces Treatment Before the advent of systemic corticosteroids, pemphigus vulgaris was usually a fatal disease; most patients died within 2–5 years of the onset of the disease because large areas of the skin lost their epidermal barrier function, leading to the loss of body fluids or to secondary bacterial infections. Systemic corticosteroid therapy, usually in the form of oral prednisone, is standard treatment. Prednisone at 1 mg/kg/day is a typical initial dosage. In general, immunosuppressive agents, such as azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil and cyclophosphamide, when combined with corticosteroids, may result in gaining early control of the disease and an increased percentage of clinical remissions. Plasmapheresis is useful for quickly reducing the titers of circulating autoantibodies and should be considered for severe pemphigus if the disease is unresponsive to a combination of prednisone and immunosuppressives. High-dose IVIg is another option for resistant disease. IVIg is a blood product prepared from pooled plasma that has immunomodulatory effects when used in a high dose. Local skin care The skin lesions are extremely painful in advanced cases. When there are extensive raw surfaces, prolonged daily baths are helpful in removing the thickened crusts and reducing the foul odour. Silver sulfadiazine (Silvadene) 1%, widely used for local therapy of burns, is an effective topical antimicrobial agent, suitable for treatment of limited disease. Management of complications of the disease; sepsis, fluid and electrolyte imbalance, hypoproteinemia. Management of complications of therapy; diabetes, hypertension, osteoporosis. Bullous pemphighoid Bullous pemphigoid (BP) is the most common autoimmune subepidermal blistering disease. BP is an example of an immune-mediated disease that is associated with a humoral and cellular response directed against two well-characterized self-antigens: BPAG2 and BPAG1 (structural components of the hemidesmosome). In the prodromal, non-bullous phase of the disease, mild to severe intractable pruritus is a consistent feature. The bullous stage of BP is characterized by the development of tense vesicles and bullae on apparently normal or erythematous skin, together with urticarial and infiltrated papules and plaques that occasionally assume an annular or figurate pattern. The blisters are tense, up to 1–4 cm in diameter, contain a clear fluid, and may persist for several days, leaving eroded and crusted areas. The diagnosis of BP is based upon the typical clinical presentation, compatible histologic features, and, most importantly, positive direct immunofluorescence (DIF) microscopy studies. In biopsy specimens of an early bulla, a subepidermal blister accompanied by a dermal inflammatory infiltrate composed of eosinophils and mononuclear cells is typically observed. The infiltrate favors the uppermost dermis, and the cavity of the bulla contains a net of fibrin with a variable inflammatory infiltrate. Treatment Oral prednisone (0.5–0.75 mg/kg/day). Immunosuppressive therapies can serve as steroid-sparing agents and are employed when corticosteroids alone fail to control the disease, there are contraindications to the use of systemic corticosteroids, and/ or comorbidities exist that limit the dosage of corticosteroid (e.g. diabetes mellitus, osteoporosis, psychosis). The most frequently employed agents are azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, methotrexate, and cyclophosphamide. Dermatitis Herpetiformis Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is a chronic, relapsing, severely pruritic disease characterized by grouped, symmetric lesion on extensor surfaces, the scalp, nuchal area, and buttocks. Pathogenesis: IgA is bound to the skin, and this apparently activates complement, primarily through the alternate pathway. This disease has an equal male-to-female incidence. The average age of onset is 20–40 years. DH has a symmetric distribution and favours the elbows, knees, extensor forearms, back, and buttocks. The primary lesions are pleomorphic, with urticarial plaques, papules, and vesicles. Grouped or “herpetiform” papulovesicles with an erythematous base are characteristic of this autoimmune disorder. Intense pruritus leads to secondary excoriation and crusting. The mucous membranes are involved in rare cases. Itching is usually intense. (Figure 8) Gluten, a protein found in cereals, except for rice and corn, provokes flares of the disease. Villous atrophy of the jejunum and inflammation of the small bowel occur. The incidence of enteropathy-associated T cell lymphoma is also increased in patients with DH and warrants increased surveillance. Differential Diagnosis Scabies: Scabies can be easily mistaken for dermatitis herpetiformis because the two conditions have features in common, polymorphic eruption namely papules, and crusted erosions in the sacral and gluteal regions and pruritus. DH often shows a symmetrical distribution of rash over extensor aspects, and a definitive diagnosis relies on a direct immunofluorescence (DIF) biopsy of unaffected skin, which reveals pathognomonic granular IgA deposits in DH but not scabies. A skin scraping for scabies can be diagnostic if mites are found. Histopathology: A subepidermal separation is noted histologically. The cellular infiltrate contains many neutrophils but may also include a few eosinophils DIF of non-involved perilesional skin reveals deposits of IgA alone or together with C3 arranged in a granular pattern at the DEJ. Treatment The drugs chiefly used for DH are dapsone and sulfapyridine. Hemolytic anemia, leukopenia, methemoglobinemia, agranulocytosis, or peripheral neuropathy may occur with dapsone. Acute hemolytic anemia (which may be severe) occurs in patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency; therefore, G6PD level should be measured before therapy For most patients, however, a gluten-free diet remains an important aspect of disease management (wheat, barley, rye).

name: PPT: SLE, Sclerderma
text: Lupus erythematosus Lupus erythematosus (LE) is usually divided into two main types: discoid LE (DLE) and systemic LE (SLE), with a third group, suba cute cutaneous LE (SCLE). Another classification: LE into three groups ; cutaneous LE, intermediate LE and SLE . DLE can be subdivided into a localized form in which lesions are confined to the face above the chin, the scalp and the ears, and a disseminated form in which lesions also occur elsewhere on the body. Discoid lupus erythematosus DLE is a benign inflammatory disorder of the skin, most frequently involving the face and scalp, and characterized by well‐defined red, scaly patches of variable size, which heal with atrophy, scar ring and pigmentary changes. DLE is one of the forms of cutaneous disease seen within the spectrum of LE: others are SCLE and acute cutaneous lupus, the latter seen in patients with the systemic form of the disease. The disease may also be more generalized, affecting areas away from the face and scalp. The incidence of cutaneous lupus was 4/100 000, with 80% being DLE. There is a peak age of onset in the fourth decade in females and slightly later in males, although it can occur at any age. The disease affects twice as many females as males. Clinical features The circumscribed or discoid form is the most frequent type of disease , and occurs particularly on the cheeks, bridge of the nose, ears, side of the neck and scalp. Cicatrical Alopecia occurs in the scalp lesions . Lesions occur as well‐defined erythematous patches, varying in size from a few millimetres to 10–15 cm. There is adherent scale in many cases, and when this is removed its undersurface shows horny plugs that have occupied dilated pilosebaceous canals. This so‐called ‘tin‐tack’ sign . Dyspigmentation occurs in patients of color. Warty lesions of LE may occur on the face and scalp. Localized cribriform scarring occurs, particularly on the face . Disseminated DLE: Characteristic lesions of DLE may occur in a widespread pat tern on the trunk and limbs, or may be localized to other body sites. This occurs most often in women, and they are usually cigarette smokers. Clinical variants : Chilblain lupus. Lupus erythematosus profundus (panniculitis). Gyrate erythema Telangectatic lupus erythematosus. Histopathology Treatment Topical potent corticosteroids. Intralesional corticosteroids. Topical calcineurin inhibitors. Oral prednisolone : a dosage of 0.5 mg/kg, rapidly tapered over 6 weeks is quickly effective. Hydroxy chloroquine: initially at 200 mg twice daily, reducing to 200 mg/day once a response is achieved. Oral thalidomide, methotrexate and mycophenolate mofetil. Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus Usually photo-aggravated and may be associated with a limited degree of systemic involvement. Clinically, patients present with non‐scarring papulosquamous eruption, usually occur above the waist and particularly around the neck, on the trunk and on the outer aspects of the arms, The borders may show vesiculation and crusting and occasionally bullae. Follicular plugging and hyperkeratosis are not prominent, heal by hypopigmentation. Other features include: Diffuse non‐scarring alopecia and photosensitivity mouth ulceration (especially of the palate), reticular livedo and periungual telangiectasia, pityriasiform lesions and erythroderma. Treatment Topical potent corticosteroids. Intralesional corticosteroids. Topical calcineurin inhibitors. Oral prednisolone . Hydroxy chloroquine. Acitretin ,isotretinoin , dapsone , oral, intravenous and subcutaneous methotrexate , thalidomide , mycophenolate mofetil , intravenous immunoglobulin and etanercept. Systemic lupus erythematosus SLE is a systemic disease characterized by multisystem organ inflammation, most commonly the skin, joints and vasculature, and associated immunological abnormalities. Females outnumber males by a ratio of approximately between 7 : 1 and 15 : 1. The peak age of onset of the first symptom or sign in females is approximately 38 years. Clinical features: Approximately 57–85% of patients have cutaneous fi ndings at some stage . Skin manifestations can present as chronic cutaneous LE (CCLE), SCLE and acute cutaneous LE (ACLE). CCLE includes localized and generalized DLE, hypertrophic LE, lupus profundus and lupus tumidus. SCLE includes annular and psoriasiform variants, acute localized and generalized LE, and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) like variants. Systemic manifestations of SLE Cutaneous manifestations with SLE Butterfly rash as part of ACLE Facial oedema Subacute cutaneous LE Chronic DLE Scarring DLE alopecia Non‐scarring alopecia Chilblain lupus Mouth ulceration Bullous eruptions Photosensitivity Raynaud’s phenomenon Chronic urticaria (>36 h) Cutaneous vasculitis Livedo reticularis Episcleritis Cheilitis Clinical features Sunlight may either precipitate or aggravate existing disease . UV radiation from fluorescent lighting and UVA from photocopiers may also cause exacerbations. although cutaneous manifestations are more common in the sum mer months and in days to weeks following UV exposure. Palmar erythema can be seen Nail changes: nail fold erythema, splinter haemorrhages, red lunulae and nail fold hyperkeratosis , Other nail findings include nail ridging, onycholysis, onychomadesis. Clinical features: Vasculitis : most commonly affects the skin, and usually presents as a palpable petechiae or purpura in dependent areas. Raynaud phenomenon : can be seen in 25–60% of patients with SLE, is characterized by reversible vasospasm of the fingers and toes, often caused by cold exposure, with triphasic color change; there is cold‐induced pallor, followed by cyanosis pain and numbness, then erythematous discoloration on rewarming. Arthritis : Involvement of the joints occurs at some time in approximately 90% of patients, arthralgia being more common than arthritis. Clinical features Pleurisy and pericarditis have a prevalence of 17% at disease onset and a cumulative incidence of 36%. Renal changes : The renal changes in SLE are very important in assessing the prognosis . Renal disease in lupus accounts for 3% of end‐stage renal failure, and is an important cause of mortality in SLE. Associations: rheumatoid arthritis, lichen sclerosus,, morphea, Sjögren syndrome , pyoderma gangrenosum. Diagnosis: Systemic Lupus International Collaborating Clinics classification criteria for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), 2012. Classify a patient as having SLE if he or she satisfies four of the clinical and immunological criteria, including at least one clinical criterion, or if he or she has biopsy‐proven nephritis compatible with SLE in the presence of ANAs or anti‐dsDNA antibodies. Investigations Biopsy for DIF. CBC: (In autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (AIHA), a positive direct antiglobulin test (Coombs’ test) in the context of haemolyic anaemia generally confirms the diagnosis ), leukopenia, anemia, thrombocytopenia. ANAs: (homogeneous pattern, speckled pattern, nucleolar pattern, peripheral or membranous pattern ). Anti ds DNA Abs: independent predictor of moderate to severe SLE flares. Serum C3. Anti Smith (anti‐Sm) antibodies are present in approximately 30% of patients with SLE. Anti‐Ro antibody occurs in approximately 30–40% of patients. Treatment Potent topical corticosteroids for skin lesions. Systemic antimalarials: hydroxychloroquine. Systemic corticosteroids. Methotrexate, cyclophosphamide, mycophenolate mofetil. Azathioprine. Intravenous immunoglobulin. Plasmapheresis. Biological drugs to treat lupus, including rituximab (monoclonal antibody to CD20). Systemic Sclerosis Systemic sclerosis is a multisystem autoimmune disease that causes fibrosis in the skin and internal organs with associated vascular and inflammatory manifestations including the Raynaud phenomenon. It has high mortality due to cardiac, pulmonary and renal complications and substantial morbidity from pain, digital ulceration, calcinosis, telangiectasias and gastrointestinal tract and musculoskeletal involvement. Most often seen in young and middle‐aged adults. Overall, there is a 4 : 1 female predominance of SSc. Clinical features: Skin manifestations include thickening or fibrosis, mostly over the extremities and face in limited forms of ssc and much more extensively in diffuse cases. Associated features include severe pruritus, digital ulceration, vascular abnormalities including telangiectasia, calcinosis, diffuse hyperpigmentation and ‘salt and pepper’ dyspigmentation. Raynaud phenomenon and symptoms of gastro‐oesophageal reflux. Non‐pitting digital oedema. Investigations Antitopoisomerase 1 antibody (anti‐scl‐70 or ATA), Anticentromere antibody (ACA), Anti‐RNA polymerase III antibody (ARA or RNAP). ECG. High‐resolution CT scan. MRI. Associated diseases Other autoimmune disease, ex: thyroiditis, RA, SLE. Overlap connective tissue disorders: ex: mixed connective tissue disease. Malignancies. Treatment is a complex process and requires a multidisciplinary approach. Methotrexate or MMF . Cyclophosphamide. N‐acetylcysteine , chlorambucil , interferon γ , minocycline. UVA1 phototherapy . Rituximab . Morphea Is a localized forms of scleroderma. which do not usually involve internal organs such as the lungs, heart and kidneys. It can occur at any age. Most studies suggest that morphoea is commoner in women, with female to male ratios of between 7 : 1 and 2.6 : 1. Types Limited plaque morphoea Single or multiple round to oval lesions >1 cm in diameter in up to two anatomical regions. May be oedematous, erythematous to bruise‐like, yellowish white, indurated with a lilac ring, or atrophic and pigmented. Involves epidermis and dermis. Guttate morphoea Multiple small erythematous to yellowish white, round to oval lesions, usually on the trunk. Involves the papillary and superficial dermis. Linear morpheoa Mostly unilateral, bilateral involvement occurs in 5–25% of cases . linear morphoea appears to follow Blaschko lines. The head variant includes morphoea en coup de sabre (ECDS) and progressive hemifacial atrophy (PHA), also known as Parry Romberg syndrome. It has a sudden onset and rapidly progressive course. Disseminated plaque morphoea : Occurrence of multiple plaques of morphoea at three or more anatomical sites Isomorphic pattern: plaques coalesce in the inframammary area in the back , waistband and around the hips and inguinal regions at sites of repeated minor trauma from clothing. Non‐isomorphic pattern: multiple individual plaques occur in a usually symmetrical distribution on the trunk and limbs. Deep involvement may occur. Investigations MRI and CT scan to assess the extent of involvement. Treatment Systemic corticosteroids. Methotrexate. Ciclosporine. MMF. UVA1 phototherapy. Topical corticosteroids/ topical viamin D analogues. Intralesional corticosteroids. References Lipsker D. name: PPT: Psoriasis
text: Psoriasis Psoriasis Is a chronic , inflammatory and proliferative disease of the skin. With multiple organ affection. The most characteristic lesions consist of red, scaly, sharply demarcated, indurated plaques, present particularly over the extensor surfaces and scalp. The extent and severity varies enormously over time and between individuals. Morphological variants are common. Both genetic and environmental influences have a critical role in the aetiology and pathogenesis. Epidemiology: There are two peak ages of incidence, the first occurring between 16 and 22 years and the second between 57 and 62 years of age. Psoriasis affects adult men and women equally. Aetiology: Genetics: Based on population data, lifetime risks of psoriasis are 4%, 28% and 65% if neither, one or both parents are affected. Environmental factors: upper respiratory streptococcal infections may precipitate guttate psoriasis. Medications: Many drugs have been reported to be responsible for the onset and/or exacerbation of psoriasis. Both cigarette smoking and alchohol misuse are associated with developing severe forms of psoriasis. Aetiology: The most important drugs involved in exacerbating psoriasis are : Lithium. Antimalarials. Interferon gamma. Beta blockers. ACE inhibitors. NSAIDS. Although psoriasis may respond to oral corticosteroids, both tachyphylaxis and rebound phenomena occur. Withdrawal of corticosteroids may lead to rebound of the disease and the development of unstable psoriasis. Aetiology: Psychological stress: Moderate to severe psoriasis is associated with increased levels of depression, anxiety . Photoexposure: Although sunlight is generally beneficial, in 5–20% of patients psoriasis may be provoked by sunlight . Trauma: Psoriasis can occur in sites of cutaneous trauma and old scars, the so‐called Koebner phenomenon: appearance of isomorphic lesions on apparently normal skin following trauma during the active stage of the disease. Pathogensis: The pathological abnormalities in psoriasis include hyperproliferation of the epidermis, a marked dermal and epidermal inflammatory infiltrate, increased angiogenesis within the dermis and abnormal cutaneous neuronal/neurotransmitter organization. Normal basal keratinocytes proliferate, differentiate and ascend through the layers of the epidermis in a process takes that approximately 30 days in healthy individuals. In psoriasis, this process only 4–5 days in active plaques. activated T cells are key in the pathogenesis of psoriasis. Pathogensis: Injury to the skin leads to activation of AMPs that binds to toll like receptors causing activation of dendritic cells that produces TNF‐α, IL‐6 and IL‐23. This results in activation of Th17 cells, which in turn activate keratinocytes to proliferate and produce multiple chemokines and antimicrobial peptides . In psoriasis plaques there are increased levels of IL‐2, IL‐8, interferon‐γ, γ TNF‐α, IL‐15, IL‐17, IL‐22 and IL‐23 . Histopathology Epidermal changes: There is parakeratosis . Focal orthokeratosis . Accumulation of neutrophils in the stratum corneum (munro microabscesses). Near absence of the granular layer ( agranulosis, hypogranulosis). Spongiform pustules in the malpighian layer Regular Hyperplasia of the malpigian layer with elongation of rete ridges ( test tube acanthosis). Suprapapillary epidermal thinning Histopathology Dermal changes: Dilated, tortuous papillary blood vessels almost touch the undersurface of the thinning suprapapillary epidermis Prescence of a mixed mononuclear and neutrophil infiltrate, as well as extravasated erythrocytes in the dilated cappillaries. Clinical picture: Plaque psoriasis: Is the most common type of psoriasis, accounting for about 80–90% of all cases . Typical lesions are red scaly plaques, which are remarkably well demarcated from unaffected skin, with sharply delineated edges plaques may be encircled by a clear peripheral zone, the halo or ring of woronoff , dusky red in colour and covered with silvery white lamellar scales. Usually bilateral symmetrical distribution, variable in size. Over the scalp, trunk and extensor surfaces of the limbs. The successive removal of scales usually reveals an underlying smooth, glossy red membrane with small bleeding points where the thin suprapapillary epidermis has been torn off (Auspitz’s sign). Scalp psoriasis: The whole scalp may be diffusely involved, or multiple discrete plaques of varying size may be seen . Very thick plaques can develop, especially at the occiput. Plaques tend to be restricted to hair‐bearing areas, extending a short distance beyond the hairline and around the ears. Seborrhoeic psoriasis (sebopsoriasis): Plaques of thin sharply demarcated erythema with variable scale may occur in the typical distribution of seborrhoeic der matitis, involving paranasal areas, external ears, medial eye brows, hairline, presternal and interscapular chest wall . Flexural psoriasis (inverse psoriasis): Psoriasis involving the inguinal creases, axillae, submammary folds, gluteal cleft, umbilicus and other body folds. Flexural involvement is often seen in individuals with plaque psoriasis elsewhere on the skin. Flexural plaques are thin, scaling is greatly reduced or absent. The surface has a glazed hue and fissuring at the depth of the skin fold is common, especially in the gluteal cleft. Non‐pustular palmoplantar psoriasis : Psoriasis may present as typical scaly patches on which a fine silvery scale can be evoked by scratching; as less well‐defined plaques. A sharply defined edge at the wrist, forearm or palm and absence of vesiculation are helpful to distinguish from eczema. Nail psoriasis : The nails grow more quickly in patients with psoriasis . Nail dystrophy may be seen in association with all types of psoriasis or occasionally as an isolated feature. Estimates of its incidence vary considerably. nail changes are present in about 40% of cases at any point in time. Psoriasis may affect any part of the nail unit, including the nail matrix, nail bed and hyponychium. Nail psoriasis is associated with more extensive psoriasis, longer disease duration, family history of psoriasis and the presence of psoriatic arthritis. Nail matrix disease presents with pits, ridges and grooves of the nail plate. Pitting is the most frequent change seen in fingernails, individual pits being uniform in size at about 1mm diameter and sometimes arranged longitudinally. Nail bed disease can be seen as subungual ‘oil drops’ which are highly specific for psoriasis. Nail bed disease also causes subungual hyperkeratosis, splinter haemorrhages and distal onycholysis. Mucosal lesions Geographic tongue (benign migratory glossitis) and fissured tongue are both more frequent among patients with psoriasis than healthy controls . Acute guttate psoriasis: This describes the sudden onset of a shower of small lesions, appearing diffusely over the body. It is more common in children and young adults in whom it may be the first presentation of psoriasis. It frequently follows several weeks after phanyngitis caused by group A streptococci, serological evidence for which can be found in about 60% of individuals. The lesions are from 2 or 3 mm to 1 cm in diameter, round or slightly oval. They are scattered more or less evenly over the body, particularly on the trunk and proximal part of the limbs, with minimal scales. Erythrodermic psoriasis Erythrodermic psoriasis, in which most or all of the body surface is affected by psoriasis, is uncommon, occurring in 1–2% of patients. Psoriasis has been found to be the underlying cause in about 25% of cases of erythroderma . It is often precipitated by environmental or therapeutic triggers including systemic illness, alcoholism, antimalarials, irritating topical treatments, ultraviolet radiation or by withdrawal of systemic corticosteroids. The patient may be febrile and systemically ill. Dependent oedema is common. Itching is often severe. Erythrodermic psoriasis Complications are those of skin failure, including sepsis, hypothermia or hyperthermia, hypoalbuminaemia, anaemia, dehydration and high output cardiac failure. Linear and segmental psoriasis : True linear or segmental psoriasis, in which lesions are unilateral or Blaschko linear, is extremely unusual. PUSTULAR PSORIASIS Neutrophil accumulation in the epidermis is a histological feature of all types of psoriasis, but in clin ical practice the term ‘pustu lar psoriasis’ is reserved for those forms of the disease in which macroscopic pustules appear. Acute generalized pustular psoriasis (von Zumbusch). Localized pustular psoriasis: (i) Palmoplantar pustulosis. (ii) Acrodermatitis continua of Hallopeau. Complications and co‐morbidities In the acute phase, the affected individual is systemically unwell. Hypovolaemia and oligaemia can cause acute kidney injury. Hypoalbuminaemia because of a sudden loss of plasma protein into the tissues and intestinal malabsorption . Hypocalcaemia may arise as a consequence of the hypoalbuminaemia and malabsorption . The absorption of therapeutic drugs may also be impaired. Abnormalities of liver enzymes are common, occurring in up to a half of patients during the acute episode . Cholestatic jaundice may arise as a consequence of neutrophilic cholangitis. Acute respiratory distress syndrome, Palmoplantar pustulosis This is a common condition in which erythematous and scaly plaques studded with sterile pustules persist on the palms or soles. Acrodermatitis continua of Hallopeau PSORIATIC ARTHRITIS Psoriatic arthritis is a seronegative inflammatory arthritis, which occurs in up to 40% of patients with moderate to severe psoriasis. It can be destructive to joints. Predominantly affecting the distal interphalangeal joints. Symmetrical rheumatoid‐like pattern, arthritis mutilans. Axial disease with spondylitis and/or sacro‐iliac disease. There is an association between more severe cutaneous psoriasis and the development of psoriatic arthritis. The prevalence of psoriatic arthritis is also increased in patients with nail and scalp psoriasis. D.D.: Topical treatment: Topical therapies are the mainstay of treatment for psoriasis of limited extent. Topical corticosteroids: Potent and very potent topical corticosteroids are the most effective . Mild to moderate potency corticosteroids are the treatment of choice on the face and neck, flexures and genitalia. The combination of a potent topical corticosteroid with calcipotriol provides the most effective strategy for topical treatment of limited plaque psoriasis. The potential side effects of topical corticosteroids are well known and include cutaneous atrophy ,tachyphylaxis, rebound flare and systemic absorption. Vitamin D analogues Calcitriol and synthetic analogues as calcipotriol and tacalcitol. The mechanism of action of these agents is via vitamin D receptor‐mediated effects on the proliferation and differentiation of epidermal keratinocytes . Calcipotriol and tacalcitol have been combined with other therapies especially with topical corticosteroids. Calcipotriol ointment enhances the efficacy of PUVA and UVB phototherapy. Dithranol: antiproliferative and pro‐apoptotic effects on keratinocytes. Coal tar: mechanism of action is not fully understood. Topical retinoids: pleiotropic effects on cellular proliferation and differentiation, ex: tazarotene. Topical calcineurin inhibitors: topical immune modulators, ex: tacrolimus and pimecrolimus. Phototherapy Narrow‐band UVB: (311–313 nm) Thrice‐weekly NB‐UVB has been shown to clear psoriasis more quickly. The initial dose is based on skin phototesting and the determination of the minimal erythemal dose (MED) or on skin phototype. Due to concerns regarding increased risk of SCC, the scrotum and genital skin should be protected from irradiation. NB‐UVB causes cutaneous immunomodulation partly by increasing vitamin D and similar to PUVA induces apoptosis of T cells and reduces epidermal hyperproliferation. PUVA photochemotherapy The combination of psoralens and long‐wave ultraviolet radiation (UVA 320–400 nm). The psoralens that are commonly used are 8‐methoxypsoralen (8‐MOP), 5‐methoxypsoralen (5‐MOP) and trioxypsoralen (T‐MOP). Psoralens are used either topically or orally in combination with UVA. This modality is highly efficacious in treating psoriasis with reported clearance rates of over 90%. Systemic therapy Methotrexate: folate antagonist that inhibits DNA synthesis by dihydrofolate reductase inhibition. maximum dose of 30 mg weekly, orally, SC or IM. Ciclosporin: Ciclosporin works by inhibiting IL‐2 production by lymphocytes via calcineurin inhibition. maximum dose of 2.5- 5 mg/ kg/day. Acitretin: Acitretin is a metabolite of etretinate which was the fi rst retinoid used in the treatment of psoriasis. Acitretin binds to nuclear receptors of the steroid superfamily, which includes the vitamin D receptor. Dose: 25–50 mg/day and assessing efficacy at 4 months . Others: Apremilast , Tofacitinib , fumaric acid esters and Hydroxycarbamide (hydroxyurea) . Biological treatment TNF‐α inhibitors: IL‐12/IL‐23 p40 inhibitors: Ustekinumab . Ichthyosis vulgaris This is the commonest form of inherited ichthyosis Autosomal dominant Clinical Picture Onset: delayed onset after 3months usu early childhood Fine scales paste on the skin with variable degree of dryness esp during winter with great improvement in summer Scales are coarser on lower limb than trunk attached centrally and detached outward rim Extensor aspect of extremities are most prominent while major body folds (eg axillary fold) are spared Palmer and soles show exaggerated skin markings and mild hyperkeratosis Associated atopic manifestation and keratosis pilaris H&E: Compact orthokeratosis reduced granular cell layer Benign course improve by time limited finding in adulthood X-linked ichthyosis This condition occurs in males only from heterozygous mother as X linked recessive (exclusively affects males) Onset: Early onset before 3months Cesarean birth is typical, with failure in progression of labor because of a placental sulfatase deficiency. Dark large tan or grey scales on the limbs and anterior neck all across the trunk. It may affect the ears and face Sides of the neck are usually involved gives dirty neck /unwashed look It varies in its severity and improves in sunny weather. It changes very little with age. Palms and soles usu spared No keratosis pilaris No increased AD Extracutaneous features: Cornaeal opacaities, cryptorchidism Prognosis: Unlike ichthyosis vulgaris, X-linked ichthyosis does not improve with age, but gradually worsens in both extent and severity. Lamellar ichthyosis Autosomal recessive Present at birth as collodion membrane desquamates in 2-3 wks or appear soon after birth Involve entire cutaneous surface Scales are large, greyish brown scales, which are strikingly quadrilateral, free at the edges, and adherent in the center Hyperkeratosis of palm and sole Ectropion is almost always present Marked/massive compact orthohyperkeratosis intact granular cell layer Treatment In the milder types of ichthyosis the main treatment is regular application of moisturisers or emollients. These moisturisers are most effective when applied on wet skin within a couple of minutes of having a shower or bath. Paraffin containing emollient , urea containing creams Keratolytics creams (keratolytics, e.g. salicylic acid) are sometimes used but they can irritate the skin and can be helpful on the palms and soles. Severe types of ichthyosis, systemic retinoid (acictretin) tablet treatment may be suggested. Clinically characterized by an extreme sensitivity to ultraviolet (UV) rays from sunlight. Autosomal recessive CP 1- skin Patients have marked photosensitivity in addition to an early onset for all major types of skin cancer. Early life/ first 2ys: photosensitivity. many patients easily develop sunburns with erythema, edema and vesicles following minimal sun exposure, lentigines/freckles, mottled pigmentation. Actinic keratoses, basal cell carcinomas (BCCs), squamous cell carcinomas (SCCs), and less frequently, melanomas then develop in sun-exposed sites, also prematurely. Skin cancer before age of 10ys BCC- SCC- less frequent MM most tumours occur on H&N 2- Ocular Ocular abnormalities are almost as common as the cutaneous abnormalities, but they are strikingly limited to the anterior, UV-exposed structures of the eye (lids, cornea, and conjunctiva). Severe photophobia, keratitis, corneal opacification, and vascularization are common manifestations, while loss of eyelashes, ectropion, and SCC and melanoma of the UVR-exposed parts of the eyes are also frequently reported. 3- Systemic manifestations There is an approximately 50-fold increase in internal neoplasms, especially of the central nervous system. Neurological; progressive neural degeneration in 20% of cases. Treatment As the skin changes are all caused by UV light, complete protection from exposure to UV can prevent further skin changes completely. Protective measures include the following: All windows should be covered with UV-resistant film When outside during daylight hours, exposed skin should be covered with sunscreen. Long trousers, long sleeves and gloves should be worn together with a UV-resistant face mask Systemic retinoids can prevent appearance of new cancers yet should be used for life so risk of side effects and rebound when stopped (cancer chemoprophylaxis). Epidermolysis Bullosa Epidermolysis bullosa (EB) is a group of rare genetic disorders that have in common the formation of blisters in response to minor physical injury. The EB conditions result from genetic defects of hemidesmosomes concerned with adhesion. Loss of adhesion results in blister formation. These may occur anywhere on the body but most commonly appear at sites of friction and minor trauma such as the feet and hands. In some subtypes, blisters may also occur on mucous membranes or internal organs, such as the oesophagus, stomach and respiratory tract, without any apparent friction. Based on different sites of blister formation within the skin structure: Inherited types of epidermolysis bullosa (EB) Intraepidermal (intraepidermal separation) Junctional (lamina lucida level of the basement membrane) Dystrophic (lamina densa and sub-lamina densa level of basement membrane) Summary of the most important features of the different subtypes! Approach Skin biopsy: Analyze one specimen using electron microscopy (EM) and the other using immunofluorescent microscopy. Evaluate infection using bacterial cultures from poorly healing wounds or wounds that appear infected. DNA mutation analysis. Management There is no cure for EB. However, significant research, including gene therapy and cell-based therapy, continue in the aim to improve quality of life. Most current treatment is symptomatic. The primary aim is to protect the skin and stop blister formation, promote healing, and prevent complications. Because EB can affect so many different parts of the body, a team of medical specialists is usually required for overall care. When necessary, treatment with oral and topical medications may be prescribed to assist healing or prevent complications. 47 Gene therapy is promising. Family education Palliative treatment. Avoid trauma Gentle and proper wound care Proper nutrition. Aggressive dental intervention. Surgical intervention The following are some general measures used in caring for a patient with EB. Avoid activities that induce friction on the skin. This includes the handling of infants and children – alternative handling techniques are easily learnt from a trained health care professional. Maintain a cool environment and avoid overheating Use foam padding to help reduce friction on pieces of furniture such as beds, chairs and infant car seats Choose clothing (including nappies) and footwear that is light, has no irritating seams or detail, (eg, zips and tight elastic). Pierce, drain and dress blisters to promote healing (this should be done only by people who have received training on wound care) Many traditional adhesive tapes and dressings may be unsuitable for people with EB — especially those with the more severe forms (eg, RDEB) — as their removal can cause additional trauma to the skin. Use of advanced wound care products such as low-adherent silicone tapes and dressings is recommended. However, resourcefulness by using items readily available, such as applying additional lubrication (eg, Vaseline/paraffin oil) to some traditional wound dressings, is helpful. When EB affects other parts of the body, various cares and treatments are adopted. For example, a soft diet when the oesophagus is involved or using stool softeners for constipation, or if the patient has anal blisters. General measures Neurofibromatosis Neurofibromatoses (NF) are genetic disorders of the nervous system, which cause tumors to form on the covering of the nerves anywhere in the body at any time. Three distinct forms of NF have been identified neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2) schwannomatosis Neurofibromatosis 1 (von Recklinghausen’s disease) NF1 is caused by mutations in the NF1 gene that encodes a protein called neurofibromin, which functions as a tumour suppressor. The protein product of NF1 (neurofibromin) is involved in the negative regulation of RAS signalling. follows a pattern of autosomal dominant inheritance. Approximately 50% of NF1 cases are inherited from a parent. About 50% are due to new mutations in the NF1 gene occurring randomly at or around conception for unknown reasons. NF1 is characterized by changes in skin appearance, tumors, or bone abnormalities. Symptoms of NF1 may be evident at birth and nearly always by the time the child is 10 years old. These include: café-au-lait macules, neurofibromas, freckling in the axillae and groin, Lisch nodules, and bony defects. Nevus anemicus is also another common early finding. Café-au-lait macules (CALMs) are tan to dark brown (depending on the degree of constitutive pigmentation), uniformly pigmented macules and patches that are randomly distributed on the body, with the exception of the scalp, palms, and soles. CALMs may not be apparent at birth and frequently become more noticeable during the first year of life. “Freckling” in the axillae and groin in NF1 is referred to as “Crowe sign”. Numerous 1–3 mm brown macules (more akin to lentigines than ephelides) typically populate these intertriginous zones, the neck, and occasionally the majority of the skin surface. Lisch nodules are found in the irides of about one quarter of patients under 6 years of age and in 94% of adult patients. Neurofibromas are soft tumors that can be pushed down into the panniculus by light pressure with the finger (“buttonholing”) and spring back when released. Acromegaly, cretinism, hyperparathyroidism, myxedema, pheochromocytoma (<1%), or precocious puberty may be present. Other features: Gastrointestinal stromal tumours chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) Hypertension: essential HTN, renovascular stenosis, pheochromoctoma. Macrocephaly Learning disabilities Scoliosis, lordosis, kyphosis, pseudoarthrosis, dislocations Osteoporosis, atraumatic fractures The diagnosis of NF-1 requires two or more of the following criteria to be fulfilled: 1. Six or more café au lait macules with a greatest diameter of more than 5 mm in prepubertal individuals, and a greatest diameter of more than 15 mm in postpubertal individuals 2. Two or more neurofibromas of any type or one plexiform neurofibroma 3. Freckling in the axillary or inguinal regions 4. Optic gliomas 5. Two or more Lisch nodules 6. Distinctive osseous lesion, such as a sphenoid dysplasia or thinning of the long-bone cortex with or without pseudarthrosis. Prognosis Lifetime risks for both benign and malignant tumors are increased in NF1-affected individuals. Cutaneous or subcutaneous neurofibromas, optic nerve gliomas, dumbbell-shaped spinal cord tumors, and brain tumors represent some of the well-recognized nerve-related neoplasms. Management Annual examinations should focus on potential complications of NF. Each examination should include blood pressure measurement, assessment of the skin for typical lesions (including early or growing neurofibromas), visual acuity check, evaluation of the eyes for evidence of proptosis or strabismus, and examination of the spine and extremities for any abnormalities. Neurologic evaluation should include a careful history for headaches or motor or sensory symptoms as well as a comprehensive motor and sensory examination. Management Annual ophthalmologic examinations should check for optic nerve pallor, visual acuity changes, visual field defects, and Lisch nodules. Patients should be referred to an ophthalmologist promptly if the treating physician has any concerns about visual acuity, evidence of proptosis, or a palpebral plexiform neurofibroma obstructing vision. Resection of neurofibromas for medical or cosmetic indications. Management Resection of neurofibromas for medical or cosmetic indications. Trials of targeted therapy to reduce the growth of cutaneous neurofibromas are ongoing and are likely to result in better treatment options for severely affected patients.
